#6893. Enterprise AI Spending Outpaces Adoption Growth, Report Finds

Enterprise AI spending is growing faster than the number of organizations paying for it, according to a new Menlo Ventures report that points to a shift from buying access for employees to financing work performed by agents.

The venture capital firm's 2026 State of Enterprise AI report estimates deployment spending reached a $176.8 billion annualized run rate by September, up from $33 billion in 2025. The share of enterprises paying for AI rose from 55% to 65%.

A larger bill can reflect broader use inside an organization, but it does not independently establish that the additional work is useful or profitable.

Menlo's methodology describes revenue figures as annualized run rates. The $176.8 billion estimate therefore should not be read as $176.8 billion already spent during the first nine months of 2026.

The report also distinguishes unusually heavy spenders from the typical respondent. Average reported spending reached 4.7 times the prior year's level, while the median reached 2.2 times. That gap suggests a smaller group of large spenders drove the average substantially.

The practical implication is that an industry growth figure may be a poor benchmark for an individual organization's budget. Buyers need to understand their own workload growth and the results it produces.

"Agents are changing the economics of software," Menlo principal Derek Xiao said in the firm's announcement.

Menlo reports that agents account for 80% of tokens on OpenRouter, a service providing access to multiple models. That measures activity on one platform, rather than all enterprise AI use. Token consumption also measures processing volume, rather than completed business outcomes.

An agent that makes repeated attempts can consume more resources without delivering proportionately more value. For procurement teams, the relevant comparison is consequently the cost of completing acceptable work, including the review it requires.

Menlo estimates that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google capture 69% of enterprise AI deployment spending. That measure is distinct from their shares of enterprise language-model API spending, a narrower category. The figures should not be used interchangeably.

The report draws on a Morning Consult survey of nearly 400 U.S. enterprise decision-makers responsible for more than $4 billion in AI spending. Market totals are modeled estimates informed by surveys, public filings, and third-party reports. Menlo discloses investments in Anthropic and OpenRouter.

A separate announcement from Information Services Group describes buyers putting more emphasis on the economics and reliability of production deployments. ISG says ongoing security and observability work remains necessary as organizations scale.

That provides a useful distinction between market demand and business value. Suppliers can generate growing revenue while customers still determine which deployments justify the cost.

For enterprise leaders, the new spending estimate strengthens the case for examining usage beyond license counts. It leaves the harder purchasing question with the customer: How much worthwhile work did the increased spending actually buy?

Menlo's State of Enterprise AI report is available here.

John K. Waters is the editor in chief of a number of Converge360.com sites, with a focus on high-end development, AI and future tech. He's been writing about cutting-edge technologies and culture of Silicon Valley for more than two decades, and he's written more than a dozen books. He also co-scripted the documentary film Silicon Valley: A 100 Year Renaissance, which aired on PBS.  He can be reached at [email protected].

#6891. Why The Rings of Power Will Never Be the Same After the Season 3 Finale

A post-finale interview with the showrunners of the ‘Lord of the Rings’ series reveals what may come.

When the creators and showrunners of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power embarked on season 3, they knew the endgame from the start: The forging of the One Ring. After two seasons in the Second Age of Middle-earth, which saw almost all the other Rings of Power forged—three for Elves, seven for Dwarves, and nine for Men—it was time for Sauron to forge the one to rule them all.

“We wanted a tighter, tauter, more profound season,” says co-showrunner Patrick McKay, in an interview with Esquire. “We wanted to start with a bang and never let up. We wanted to deepen our characters psychologically, and challenge them in new ways. You’re seeing the end of one part of the story, and the beginning of another.”

“We had to have Sauron forge the One Ring,” adds J.D. Payne, who also created and serves as co-showrunner with McKay. “To do that, all the storylines in some way are connected to Sauron’s attempts at world domination. That was the one that so much of our attention and focus went into getting right, and it took all of our departments working together at the top of their games to create.”

On Wednesday, just in time for Thanksgiving, Prime Video gave Tolkien fans a feast with the final two episodes of The Rings of Power season 3: episode 7, “Orodruin,” and episode 8, “The Doom of Men.”

In the penultimate episode, Sauron (Charlie Vickers) learns from the Balrog—who talks, apparently!—how to use the fires of Mount Doom to forge the One Ring. Then, with the power of the One Ring literally in his hands, Sauron mobilizes his army for battle against Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle), the king of Númenor. But instead of a big, violent bloodbath in the spirit of, say, Game of Thrones, Sauron simply... surrenders. Or does he? We’re talking about a master deceiver, after all.

In a spoiler-filled interview with Esquire, McKay and Payne unpack a few of our biggest questions about season 3, including how and why the Balrog speaks (with actor Simon Pegg lending his voice) to why Pharazôn is actually one of the most consequential figures in the series.

This interview has been edited for clarity.

PATRICK MCKAY: One of the things we're constantly trying to do is go deeper into Tolkien’s life's work. He did not just create The Lord of the Rings, he wrote all this other stuff. He envisioned an entire world. It's his legendarium. When you do the deep dive, you find there are surprising things if you only know the book and film trilogy. The Balrog Gandalf faces down in Moria is part of this level of “super being” that is equal to Gandalf and Sauron. They’re Maiar. In prior ages, Balrogs could cast spells and command troops. They’re intelligent. They can talk, you just don’t see that one talk in that circumstance.

The idea of walking out onto a diving board and doing something risky, to show a different side of that being, was something that we felt compelled to do this season. It’s certainly unexpected. We’re always looking to do that. We don’t want to be familiar. We want to show you things in this world that you haven’t seen before.

Talk to me about designing a new One Ring. Granted, it’s a gold ring; there’s not much you can really deviate. But in what ways did you want to create a One Ring that belongs to The Rings of Power?

MCKAY: The books are pretty specific about the way it looks. It’s a plain gold band. If you’re gonna do that, it’s going to look like the One Ring you’ve seen in other adaptations. We did make a few modifications, just for camera. We broadened it to give it more chunkiness. But it is what it says on the tin.

How is season 3 a culmination of everything that’s happened before, and how is it setting up the rest of the show?

J.D. PAYNE: It pulls together everything we’ve been doing with Sauron and Galadriel from the first two seasons. In season 1, he befriended her and deceived her in the guise of Halbrand. In season 3, you see Celebrimbor tormenting him: “You’re never gonna be able to make a ring capable of dominating all the other rings—or dominating her.” Part of Sauron’s ambition to forge the One Ring, as a character motivation, is being able to dominate the person who said “no” to him over the last few seasons. You understand how crazy that must have driven him.

MCKAY: The show’s called Rings of Power, because the creation is the throughline of this entire era of Tolkien’s mythology. At the end of season 3, you’ve now seen the creation of all of them. That’s now the world we live in. Everyone in Middle-earth is a nuclear power, so to speak. Now we’re setting up for the next part of the story, which is, “What are the consequences going to be?” One thing in season 3 we really invested in was Númenor to set Sauron up as the bowling ball crashing into those pins. That’s sort of the beginning of the end of the Second Age. It’s a tragic story. The Rings have an impact on Middle-earth that is felt for thousands of years. Now they are in this world.

The finale is literally titled “The Doom of Men,” and it ends with Sauron “surrendering” to Pharazôn. Or so that’s what he wants them to think. Can you break down this moment? How is this Sauron’s big chess move?

PAYNE: Everything builds up to that. You’ve seen Gandalf getting through to the Dark Wizard and take out a massive portion of Sauron’s army at the last moment. So the game changes right from underneath him, and he has to make a calculation. Is he going to put all his chips on the table and lose his army in a stalemate? Or is there another way? The great thing about Sauron is that he’s amazing at constructing scenarios that are lose-lose. If he can’t beat Pharazôn on the field of battle, he reasons maybe there’s another way. That’s why the final moment is filled with tension. It’s not simply a surrender. Our Elves, particularly Galadriel, know Sauron so well. She knows this is not a defeat for Sauron, and he’s going to find a way to make this into a play for exactly what he wants. Those who know the lore know what happens when Sauron is taken prisoner to Númenor. We wanted that feeling of dread, watching Charlie Vickers have a hint of a smile.

One of the most consequential characters this season has been Pharazôn. In what ways does Pharazôn represent the downfall of man?

MCKAY: This is a major character in the mythology. We introduced him in season 1, he’s been sort of a politician gathering power. In season 3, he’s been king for five days, and he’s in his heyday. He’s in his golden era. But he’s driven by insecurity. There was this blacksmith we empowered, who got away, who’s now marching around saying he’s “Lord.” No, I’m the guy! There’s professional jealousy there.

We talk sometimes about how he’s Stalin to Sauron’s Hitler. You’ve got two characters who are quite full of themselves, and have a high opinion of themselves, which puts them on a trajectory. Pharazôn’s goal is, “I want to take on Sauron.” That makes him a compelling character because you watch the way he greases the wheels and maneuvers to bring about that end. We give a lot of credit to our actor, Trystan Gravelle. He leaps off the screen in season 3.

Speaking of showdowns, one of the biggest confrontations you stage in season 3 is between Sauron and Gandalf, which Tolkien never wrote in the books. What did you hope to discover by pitting these characters together?

MCKAY: The journey of Gandalf and his involvement with Ciaran Hinds’ character, Pollando, has real deep roots in some Tolkien deep cuts where he talked about wizards who went east and that their activities probably prevented the east from joining Sauron. The story comes from that. We wanted to dramatize that through some of the most iconic characters in the legendarium coming face to face.

PAYNE: Seeing the contrast between them felt like too delicious an opportunity to pass up. Sauron is seeking power at all costs, and Gandalf has been told by the Secret Fire, “To access the greatest power in the universe, you have to give up all other power.” So when Gandalf is offered the world by Sauron, he turns it down. If you demand power, it’s going to destroy you. Ultimately, having the One Ring, and forging it and trying to keep power, sets up the weaknesses of the Third Age that the heroes exploit to finally destroy Sauron.

One of my favorite hobbies is Magic: The Gathering, which has had both Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit as crossover sets. Are there any possibilities for a Rings of Power collaboration?

MCKAY: [Laughs.] No. This is the first we’ve heard about it.

PAYNE: We actually wrote a draft of a Magic: The Gathering script in the before times. It was one of the last scripts we worked on before turning to Rings of Power. But it was right before the Disney-Fox merger, and it kinda got lost there. But we love that universe.

#6890. 7 Home Organizing Trends That Will Be EVERYWHERE in 2027, According to Pros

Your clutter-free future starts with what you already own.

Although trends prevail in the interior design world, they also can find their way into other areas beyond decor—such as home organization. Creating orderly spaces can make life a lot easier. While tried-and-true solutions are still around, there are always fresh ways to tackle organizing projects.

As we look to the year ahead, four professional organizers are here to share what they think will be the top organizing trends.

While AI has been all over the place, from work to our personal lives—it appears to be tapering off, according to Lenora O’Keith, decluttering and organizing expert and owner of Aronel Home.

“AI and smart home solutions were everywhere at the beginning of the year, but there’s definitely been a lot of AI fatigue and a push for ‘dumb tech’ lately,” she shares. “When working with clients, a lot of them are over AI being added into everything. They just want simple solutions that work.” This can include things like setting up a household command center and labeling storage containers.

Moving has traditionally been a stressful experience that you were expected to figure out on your own—but that may be changing. Allison Flinn, owner of Reclaim Professional Organizing, says that more people are taking advantage of organizing services when they move.

“You can pack and unpack, but you won't truly have a fully functional and an organized new home if you haven't decluttered prior to moving or aren't intentional during the unpacking process by implementing a system that truly works for your lifestyle,” she says.

Instead of doing what a lot of us do—devising storage systems for each individual space—2027 may welcome the idea that you should treat your home as an entire unit to be organized.

Michelle Urban, owner and founder of The Organized House, says that people are increasingly not treating each room as its own one-off organizing project. She says that instead, they’re looking at how belongings move from one space to another and where they need to be throughout the day. For instance, items like backpacks, shoes, and sports gear may land in the entry, get stored in the garage, and need to be back by the door the next morning.

“When those spaces are planned together, the system supports the family’s routine instead of just moving things from one pile to another,” Urban says.

Viewed more holistically, experts are also seeing that organizing isn’t just an occasional task, but something to stay on top of each week. “I think more homeowners will begin to view organization as ongoing home maintenance rather than a one-time project,” says Ashley Bailey, founder and professional organizer at Everything Orderly. “Just like other aspects of maintaining a home, organizing requires occasional attention as our lives and needs change.”

Flinn says that more and more people are outsourcing household tasks to a home manager or home concierge. In addition to handling things like doing laundry, returning packages, and making doctor’s appointments, these professionals can also help you organize your home in just a few hours a week.

Eco-friendly everything is still as popular as ever, and it even applies to how we organize our homes. While O’Keith says that sustainability never really goes out of style, homeowners are increasingly turning to eco-friendly organizing products—specifically, by avoiding plastic and embracing natural materials like bamboo, rattan, and sea grass for baskets and bins.

But she says that there is a exception for basements and attics. “I always recommend heavy-duty plastic storage [for these areas],” O’Keith says. “Since those spaces deal with dampness, temperature changes, and pests, other materials could get damaged easily.”

While it can be lovely to live in a well-designed, beautiful home, if there isn’t function, you might make your daily life more difficult. That’s why people are going beyond Instagram-ready interiors and are wrapping in plenty of function.

Urban believes that progressively more people are bringing functional storage into a room’s design, and it isn’t just an add-on.

“A credenza can hold games in the living room; a dining room buffet can store wrapping paper and party decor between celebrations,” Urban points out. “As rooms take on more jobs, people want storage that looks like it belongs and does a useful job.”

As we head into 2027, people are thinking about their budgets more and more, which is why using items you already have as storage solutions is cost-effective.

“I'm seeing more clients interested in making better use of what they already own rather than automatically purchasing new organizing products,” Bailey says. For instance, she recently took on a project that transformed a playroom, but used items the family already had.

“Sometimes the best solution isn't another organizing product. It's rethinking how you're using the space and what you already have,” she says. “I think we'll see more emphasis on thoughtful editing and repurposing before purchasing something new.”

#6889. Phishing Threats Totaled 7.3 Billion in Q3 2026

E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

According to a report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Microsoft Defender Security Research Team, phishing detections reached nearly 3 billion in September alone.

The findings also highlighted changes in attacker techniques, including business-service impersonation, credential theft, and social engineering through Microsoft Teams.

The Redmond-based firm recognized approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services during Q3.

DocuSign was the most frequently spoofed brand in September, accounting for 29% of the month's tracked spoofing activity. Adobe, SurveyMonkey, and Barracuda also experienced increases toward the end of the quarter.

The research found that some malicious messages were delivered despite failing e-mail authentication checks and being identified as threats.

In September, tenant- or user-level security overrides applied to 63% of these messages with a recorded security outcome — most involved tenant-level exceptions.

Microsoft warned that overly broad exceptions intended to support legitimate business communications can weaken protection against impersonation attacks.

The company emphasized that these findings do not establish whether recipients opened the messages or whether accounts were compromised.

Microsoft also recorded approximately 141,000 malicious Teams call attempts during Q3.

Attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names instead of explicitly impersonating IT support personnel. Such display names accounted for 46% of an observed sample in July, rising to 88% in September.

Meanwhile, QR code phishing declined 67% compared to Q2, totaling roughly 12.1 million attacks.

CAPTCHA-gated phishing activity increased toward the end of the quarter, reaching 3.1 million detected attacks in September. SVG attachments played a significant role in the increase.

Credential theft remained the primary objective of malicious attachment campaigns, with approximately 94% to 96% of payload-based attacks directing users to phishing sites or fraudulent sign-in pages.

Microsoft recommended reviewing Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365 configurations, enabling Safe Links and Safe Attachments, and strengthening authentication protections.

The company also advised organizations to review security exceptions and verify the identities of external Teams contacts before responding to suspicious requests.

For more information, go to the Microsoft blog post.

According to a survey by data and AI services provider Further, enterprises are reporting benefits from artificial intelligence even as their data preparation and oversight processes remain incomplete.

Our nation's largest early childhood program has not fully caught up with what science now tells us about how children learn.

A recent Cloud Security Alliance report urges organizations to inventory, govern, and continuously monitor machine and agent identities.

Recent research from Thales highlights how AI adoption and emerging quantum computing threats are putting pressure on existing security measures.

#6880. Forget Plymouth Rock This Thanksgiving. American History Is Better Reflected by a Different Stone.

Instead of staring at a boulder in a hole in the ground, drive 42 minutes west to the town of Berkley, where our country’s complicated past is plain to see.

Let me send out a little Thanksgiving advice to potential tourists planning to visit us in the Commonwealth (God save it!) in the future. If some local tells you to go to see Plymouth Rock, tell them you have tickets for a four-day Duck Tour of the Freedom Trail. I promise you: Seeing Paul Revere’s house four times is infinitely more interesting than seeing Plymouth Rock once.

First of all, Plymouth Rock is a boulder in a hole in the ground. Oh, there’s a classical templish thing above it, but it’s still a boulder in a hole in the ground. Second, there’s almost no historical evidence that any pilgrim feet ever trod upon the rock in question. None of the contemporaneous accounts mention it. It was a nonagenarian named Thomas Faunce who, in 1741, 121 years after the Mayflower arrived, decided that this was the rock on which all the Bradfords and their shipmates disembarked. It moved around Plymouth a lot in the early years. In 1774, it cracked in two, which some folks took as an ill omen for the burgeoning Revolution. (Pieces of it are in the Smithsonian) The year 1620 was carved into the boulder’s surface in 1880. In 1920, it found its permanent home. In 1990, writing in The New Yorker, John McPhee wrote of the rock:

Even Alexis de Tocqueville, America’s greatest tourist and, therefore, its primordial sucker, fell for the Rock’s charisma.

Damn, Alexis. Have some Madeira and chillez out, mon ami.

If you want to see a genuinely interesting boulder, drive 42 minutes west to the town of Berkley, where you will find Dighton Rock State Park. In another templish building, there is Dighton Rock. It is a six-sided, five-foot-high slab of sandstone. It is also adorned with ancient petroglyphic carvings of uncertain origin. There are depictions of animals and an assortment of lines and whorls and mysterious designs. In 1680, John Danforth got a look at the Dighton Rock and not even his recently bestowed Harvard degree could explain them. He made drawings of the carvings he could see. (At the time Danforth saw it, the rock was partially submerged in the Taunton River.) It also drew the interest of local celebrities like Cotton Mather and poet James Russell Lowell.

Danforth’s opinion was that the carvings were made by the local Native tribes, and he thought it depicted an ancient battle of some sort. (If there’s anything like a consensus among people who have studied the carvings, it’s Danforth’s.) However logical that might seem, it didn’t tamp down speculation as the years went by. Down through the centuries, the carvings have been attributed to Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Vikings, Portuguese adventurers, Chinese explorers, and Japanese mariners. And, of course, inevitably … aliens.

However, it was a professor of psychology from Brown University who had the right of it, I think. Edmund Delabarre was a well-respected psychological researcher in the first half of the 20th century. He also grew fascinated with the study of rock carvings in and around Narragansett Bay. Ultimately, his researches brought him to the shores of the Taunton River and to the Dighton Rock.

Ultimately, Delabarre dismissed all the other claims of origin and concluded that the carvings on the Dighton Rock were probably made by a crew sailing under the command of one Miguel Corte-Real, a Portuguese explorer who charted about 600 miles of coastline in and around the Canadian Maritimes. In 1502, Corte-Real set sail for the western Atlantic, seeking to discover what had become of his brother, Gaspar, who had not returned from a voyage to Newfoundland. Miguel vanished, too.

Delabarre’s contention was that Miguel had made it to New England, and he argued that the inscription was a form of abbreviated Latin that proclaimed Corte-Real to be “king of the Indians.” In his 2017 book The Place of Stone, Douglas Hunter pretty much demolished all of the outre interpretations of the carvings, arguing that the carvings were of Native origin, and that the other interpretations were elements in the erasure of Native history and the legacy of bloody colonization, of which, ironically, the settlement at Plymouth was Ground Zero. The people who didn’t step onshore on a rock in Plymouth launched one of the first campaigns of the greater American genocide. As Hunter wrote:

So there’s American history on the Thanksgiving of 2026, ground up between two stones, one a legend with a counterfeit past, and another a mystery with a stolen past. The latter is by far the more compelling. Its history encompasses all of the history, good and bad, of this appropriated continent. Edmund Delabarre was wrong about Miguel Corte-Real and the Portuguese, but he might have been more right than he knew when he wrote that Dighton Rock was a kind of test. In the ambiguity of its carvings at the time of Delabarre’s work, a person saw in them what he wanted to see. Not all of it was pretty, or ennobling, or triumphal. But it's all ours.

#6878. 5 Thanksgiving Hosting Tips That’ll Make Your Dinner Parties Feel More Special Any Time of Year

Experts say the secret is using what you love—and skipping what you don’t.

For many households, Thanksgiving is the main hosting event they look forward to all year. But what is it about this holiday that makes it such an annual highlight, and how can you emulate that same essence more than just once a year?

We reached out to entertaining experts to learn which Thanksgiving hosting tips you can apply to year-round gatherings. These are the lessons that will make even your most laid-back get-togethers all the more memorable.

According to Whitney Ray, owner of Wyeth Ray Interiors, one reason that hosting Thanksgiving feels so special is that it's the one time of year most hosts actually break out their nice tableware. However, she believes you should be using these beautiful and sentimental pieces more often.

"So many people wait to use their best serving and dinnerware pieces at holidays like Thanksgiving, but I say those beautiful dishes should be used all year long," she says. "A Tuesday night dinner with a few friends doesn’t need to be formal, but mixing your nice china with your everyday pieces elevates a normal night into something more."

Hovik Harutyunyan is an event designer, etiquette specialist, and the founder of Harutyunyan Events. He believes that one key logistical trick a host can apply to any dinner or party they host is curating a menu full of familiar foods that are easy to prepare ahead.

"Thanksgiving menus work so well because the recipes are familiar as well as tried-and-true," he says. "For example, let's talk about the pies. Thanksgiving dessert is so easy because most of us opt for pumpkin and pecan pie. We know the dessert, and it's extremely easy to make in advance."

He also notes that it's best not to try out complicated, brand-new recipes for a big hosting event. You should opt for an elevated menu that is easy to scale and distribute across a large number of guests.

Thanksgiving is one meal where guests love contributing by bringing a side dish or dessert. While not every gathering needs to have a potluck element, there are other ways you can lighten your cooking load.

Christina Samatas and Renee DiSanto are principals of Park & Oak, and DiSanto is also the owner of Marcel’s Culinary Experience, a culinary community and cooking school. Both of them fully endorse taking a few shortcuts when it comes to hosting any big dinner.

"Not every detail needs to be homemade to feel special," DiSanto says. "There are many ways to save you a few steps, such as using pre-cut veggies or incorporating a few prepared appetizers or sides. Spend more time on the details that matter the most to you, rather than the little things."

For any event you hold, it's pretty much inevitable that guests always end up in the kitchen. "Whether you invite guests in or not, Thanksgiving shows us the kitchen is where people naturally congregate before a meal, whether they are wanting to help or simply catch up before dinner is served," Ray says.

For this reason, she says you should always plan to entertain in the kitchen at any gathering. Consider adding small bites and a drinks station on your kitchen counter or island, and try to clean as you go while making the meal.

Thanksgiving is a celebration of gratitude, and Harutyunyan believes you should apply the same spirit to any party. Anytime you gather with loved ones is an opportunity to give them a special experience.

"Thanksgiving, and the holidays in general, is one of the most magical times of the year," he says. "As stressful and chaotic as they may be, we love to gather with our loved ones to enjoy each other's company. We share stories, memories, and gratitude. The holiday spirit takes over all of us, which is what drives us to create such fabulous dinner spreads, decorate the home, and create an intentional experience for those on the guest list."

#6872. The Case for Ending a Relationship Even When Nothing Is Wrong With It

During my sophomore year of high school, in the throes of the COVID-19 pandemic, I started a relationship with my first love. While I am known to be a Type A planner, I tried to live in the moment, experiencing all the butterflies, first-times, and ups and downs of adolescent affection, just like my idols in the best coming-of-age movies.

It wasn’t until the start of the college application process, two years later, that my love-blinded bubble popped and I realized we simply wanted different things. But looking back, I wonder how much of my break up decision was about the relationship itself, and how much was about the life I was looking forward to in college and beyond.

I think that’s common for a lot of young people in relationships. Many of us break up at young ages not because there’s something wrong with the other or the dynamic—there's no cheating, no explosive fight, and no obvious villain—but because we feel like we should. I’ve witnessed friends who are perfectly happy together in their early 20s call it quits for the fear of missing out on the future experiences that are a fundamental part of being young.

If I’m being honest, I think it’s good to expand your dating portfolio before finding your forever love; there's great value in diversifying. Different relationships introduce us to different versions of ourselves, revealing what we need, what we're willing to compromise on, what we never want to experience again and simply what we do and don’t lie. And while I admire the people who are “one and done,” I can't help but wonder how you could know what you want forever if you've only ever known one version of someone—mainly yourself.

In relation to my first love, I knew I was ready to end things, but remained in limbo for months. Not only was that a waste of his time, but it was stupid to waste my own. Looking back, I don't regret the relationship, nor do I regret leaving it. Since then, I've loved and been loved by different people, for different reasons, and learned something new about myself each time. I'm not saying you have to date half of your city before settling down, or that those who stay with their first love are missing out. For some couples, growing up together is precisely what makes their relationship so special and I would never knock something like that. But I do believe there’s also value in choosing to leave a relationship even if there isn’t anything wrong with it—not for the reason that it’s all you’ve ever known, but because you realize you want to know more.

#6870. ‘I’m Excited to F*ck People Who Read’: Inside the New Dating App for Book Lovers

Readme wants to make modern dating more intellectually stimulating.

It was nearly 10:00 p.m. on a busy Thursday night in New York City when four young women brushed past a security guard at Funny Bar, a sexy late-night steakhouse, and crashed their way into the party. They made a beeline for the dance floor, knocking into me. Vodka splashed from my martini glass. This was the launch party for Readme, a dating app for readers.

Until the interlopers arrived, the room had been inundated with writers, publishers, podcasters, and other social intellectuals—people who loved to read or pretended they do. Now it was reaching full tilt. I squeezed between partygoers to ask Caroline Calloway—socialite, author of the memoir Scammer, and Readme creative director—about her involvement with the app. “I’m so ready for the dating-app space to not be such a hellscape,” she told me. “I’m more excited than ever to fuck people who are able to read.”

That is the promise of Readme. It aims to be an oasis among the swamp of dating apps where likeminded people can find someone intellectually stimulating that they want to fuck—or at least date a couple times. Dating apps like Hinge, Tinder, and the various off-shoots just aren’t cutting it anymore. A recent Match Group report found that 78 percent of users felt burned-out from the apps, and the number of people who pay for dating apps is declining. Nearly every single person I know who’s still on the apps tells me they never actually talk to anyone out there. That’s where Readme comes in.

“Everyone knows that the existing dating-app culture is deeply unsatisfying overall,” Emily Segal, the head of brand at Readme, says. “It often makes people feel overly performative, transactional, or disposable. We realized that when someone’s taste in books and literature resonates with you, you feel seen on a much deeper level.”

Or, as Calloway told me, “Out of my four major loves, the two that were built on intellectual respect were a lot deeper.”

The tagline for Readme is that it’s for “people whose love language is language,” and it comes at a precarious time for readers. We’re in what many have dubbed the postliterate age. Reading for pleasure has fallen from 28 percent in 2004 to 16 percent in 2023. Most of us would rather doomscroll than crack open a book.

Bypassing the superficiality of modern dating apps by making singles engage with their literary side seems like a novel (pun intended) solution. The app works by taking a detailed account of people’s compatibility. Readme creators Banu Gular and Segal were also behind Co-Star, the astrological-compatibility app with more than 30 million registered users worldwide. When you create an account on Readme, you have to fill out a lengthy quiz that will result in your taste profile. “You answer questions about the books and writing you like, and it gives you a portrait of your taste in language, which we think reflects how you approach love,” Segal says. “The app gives you a portrait of your literary taste and how you see the world, which we call an archetype. You’ll see a snippet of someone’s archetype when you match with them and some information about how you might get along—how you use the information is up to you.”

Back at the launch party, I met a guy who had just moved to New York City and came as a friend’s plus-one. As I quizzed him on his recent reads, Gloria Steinem came up, and to my utter horror, he didn’t know who she was. Desperate to redeem himself, he admitted he was a big Joan Didion fan; his ex introduced him to her writing. Maybe there is hope.

#6862. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6855. James Talarico’s Political-Powerhouse Girlfriend, Brianna Menard, Is Also a Master Thrifter

The 2026 midterm elections brought a blue wave of record-breaking wins. Among the most monumental was James Talarico, who became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Texas since 1988.

But his historic win is not all the internet has been talking about. At his celebratory Election Night event in Austin, Texas, the 37-year-old senator-elect was joined by his girlfriend, Brianna Menard, who was previously his chief of staff. Days later, the two attended a University of Texas football game—to which Menard wore a corduroy minidress she thrifted the week before—and the moment went viral across social media. (Even better, Talarico’s mom was the one who shared the photo of the couple at the game that quickly got traction on X.)

Chalk it up to her political prowess, clear sense of style, or the fact that she looks like an Instagram baddie, but some fans have even gone as far as to declare the pair this generation’s John F. Kennedy and Jacqueline Kennedy.

The couple first met in 2022, when Menard joined the politician’s team as chief of staff, and their relationship eventually turned romantic. Menard has been by Talarico’s side throughout his Senate campaign, accompanying him to the polls on Election Day in November and later joining him onstage to celebrate his historic victory.

So, who is Brianna Menard? Ahead, everything to know about Talarico’s accomplished and stylish girlfriend.

Menard is a born-and-raised Texan. She attended and graduated from the University of Texas at Austin, where she studied government.

In 2022, Menard was hired as Talarico’s chief of staff. According to reports, the two didn’t begin dating until a year later, after which Menard left her role working for the politician. In August 2026, Talarico’s campaign confirmed the couple’s relationship. “Four years ago, after he and his then-chief of staff developed feelings for each other and started dating, she left the office to pursue other opportunities,” a Talarico campaign spokesman told the New York Times.

After leaving Talarico’s office, Menard worked on the campaign for Rep. Salman Bhojani, the first Muslim member of the Texas legislature, and eventually became his chief of staff.

Menard is currently the director of TEXPAC and political education at the Texas Medical Association. According to her bio on the organization’s site, before stepping into the role, she had a decade of experience working in the Texas Legislature and previously served as executive director of the Early Childhood Caucus of the Texas House, where she led bipartisan efforts to “advance early learning, childcare access, workforce development, and healthcare affordability.”

Menard’s bio also lists her as the Board Secretary for Wheatsville Food Co-op and a member of the City of Austin’s Early Childhood Council.

According to a now-deleted bio on the Wheatsville Food Co-Op site, where she currently serves as Board Secretary, Menard called herself a “foodie and a committed vegan” who loves cooking. In the welcome post, she also revealed her love of yoga, dancing, and cuddling her cat named Zia.

“I’ve spent my career serving in the Texas Legislature and working on political campaigns across the state with the goal of making Texas a healthier and more equitable home for all of us,” she wrote in the post.

Menard joined Talarico at the polls to vote early in the midterm elections. On November 3, she also joined Talarico’s Election Night event in Austin, where she congratulated the Senator-elect on stage following his historic win. The couple shared a sweet hug and kiss to celebrate.

#6854. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6843. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

One year earlier, the actress told The New Yorker, “Everything bounced back, pretty much, after the first one. Second one, nothing bounced back.”

While fans aren’t exactly sold on Lawrence’s denial of a bleph, makeup artists often do have tricks up their sleeves for faking an eyelid lift. For starters, placement matters. When emphasizing the crease, apply shadow above the natural crease. “I like patting shadows onto the lid first, then blending the edges after. Too much back-and-forth blending can make the shape disappear,” celebrity makeup artist Christian Briceno previously told Bazaar. Also, opt for an elongated look, like a soft wing, to make the eye look instantly bigger. This also applies to mascara—artists recommend focusing application on the outer corners versus the center.

#6829. So, You Want to Tie Someone Up During Sex

Consider this your beginner’s guide to bondage, minus the complicated knots.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Being tied up during sex sounds pretty hot in theory, but the logistics of actually making it happen? Slightly less hot. What are you supposed to use? Where do your hands go? And how do you tell your partner you'd like to be temporarily relieved of all decision-making responsibilities in the bedroom without making it a whole thing?

Fortunately, experimenting with bondage doesn't have to involve a complicated rope setup or a trip to the hardware store (in fact, please skip the latter).

“You don’t need to rush to the most elaborate version of bondage to make it hot,” says Lisa Opel, the resident sex educator at MYLO.

Even the simplest forms of bondage, though, require a little more communication than your average hookup. Whether you're interested in doing the tying, being the one who's tied up, or taking turns, a little preparation goes a long way.

Below, sex experts break down how to tie someone up during sex, what to use (and what to leave in your junk drawer), and how to explore bondage safely without getting in over your head.

Bondage is a form of consensual play that involves restricting someone's movement. It's the “B” in BDSM, but you don't necessarily have to be into pain, punishment, or even dominance and submission to enjoy it.

“People enjoy rope play for all kinds of reasons: the feeling of surrender, the trust and power exchange, the anticipation, restriction, or simply because it feels meditative, pleasurable, or playful,” says Wildilisa Moronta, a relationship therapist and sex expert at Taimi.

For the person being restrained, part of the appeal might be relinquishing control or experiencing familiar sensations in a new way. For the person doing the restraining, it might be the excitement of taking charge or building anticipation for their partner. And for some people, the visual alone is a major turn-on.

Bondage can be as simple as wearing a pair of soft cuffs or as elaborate as practicing shibari, a form of rope bondage with Japanese roots. Some people even enjoy rope bondage as an artistic practice outside of sex, says Moronta.

Basically, there's no minimum level of kinkiness required to enjoy bondage. You can be perfectly content with a pair of quick-release cuffs and never feel the urge to pick up a rope.

You don't have to go from zero to a full-blown BDSM scene the first time you experiment with bondage. Both Moronta and Opel recommend keeping things simple and getting comfortable with the experience before introducing anything more complicated. Here's how to get started:

Before anyone breaks out the handcuffs, make sure you're working with the same definition of bondage. “One person might be imagining wrists in cuffs while kissing; the other might be picturing pain, control, or a much more intense scene,” says Opel.

Discuss who wants to be restrained, what kinds of touch you're comfortable with, and what your hard and soft limits are. You'll also want to talk about any injuries or joint issues that could make certain positions uncomfortable. Establish a safeword and discuss how you'd like to communicate throughout the experience.

You don't need anything particularly elaborate for your first experience with bondage. Opel recommends soft or padded cuffs with quick-release fastenings designed specifically for bondage, since they're easier to remove.

If you're specifically interested in rope bondage, both experts recommend taking a class with a qualified instructor before attempting any knots on a partner. Whatever restraints you choose, make sure you know how to remove them quickly before using them.

You can experiment with the feeling of bondage without actually tying anyone up. Moronta suggests loosely draping a scarf or rope over your partner's wrists while they're sitting or lying comfortably, without securing it or restricting their movement. It's a low-pressure way to figure out whether the sensation and dynamic appeal to you both.

If you're ready to experiment with actual restraints, Opel recommends starting with soft, quick-release cuffs around the wrists, keeping your partner's hands in front of their body rather than behind their back. There's no need to attempt complicated positions, especially ones that put unnecessary strain on the shoulders or joints. The experience should be about enjoying the sensation of restraint, not testing anyone's flexibility.

If you're the person doing the tying, you're responsible for more than setting the mood. You also need to pay attention to your partner's physical and emotional comfort and be prepared to release them immediately.

If you're the person being tied up, think about what appeals to you and what might make you uncomfortable. Maybe you love the idea of relinquishing control but get anxious when you can't move freely. Communicate those feelings to your partner, and speak up if something doesn't feel right.

Giving up control doesn't mean giving up your ability to make decisions. You're allowed to change your mind at any point, even if the experience was your idea in the first place.

Checking in doesn't have to take you out of the moment. “A quiet ‘How are you feeling?’ can help someone feel safe enough to relax and surrender,” says Moronta.

“The restrained person shouldn’t have to carry all the responsibility for saying when something is wrong,” adds Opel. Rather than relying on a safeword alone, ask specific questions about your partner's physical comfort and pay attention to changes in their behavior. If something seems off, pause and check in.

When you're finished, remove the restraints and spend some time checking in with each other. What that aftercare looks like will depend on what you both need.

“That might be a cuddle, water, a blanket, space, reassurance, or just a very normal conversation,” says Opel.

It's also worth talking about what you enjoyed, what you didn't, and whether you'd want to do anything differently next time. You might discover that you love bondage, that you prefer being restrained to doing the restraining (or vice versa), or that you'd rather leave it in the realm of fantasy.

As much fun as bondage can be, restricting someone's movement comes with very real physical risks. And just because a restraint looks comfortable doesn't necessarily mean it is.

“A common suggestion is to see whether you can slide a finger beneath a tie, but that doesn’t prove the tie is safe or rule out nerve pressure,” says Moronta.

Keep restraints away from the neck, avoid positions that restrict breathing, and be mindful of pressure on joints, nerves, and blood vessels. Both experts recommend leaving suspension, weight-bearing ties, and complicated rope work to people who've received proper training.

To keep things safe, both experts also recommend the traffic light system for safewords: Green means you're comfortable continuing, yellow means slow down or check in, and red means stop and release. If speaking might be difficult, establish a nonverbal signal beforehand that the restrained person can reliably make and their partner can easily recognize. If you can't establish a reliable way to communicate, don't restrict your partner's ability to speak or signal.

During play, Opel recommends asking specific questions, like whether anything feels too tight or whether your partner is experiencing any tingling or pain. Numbness, burning, weakness, dizziness, loss of movement, and difficulty breathing are all signs to stop and release the restraints immediately. Seek emergency medical help for difficulty breathing or other severe symptoms, and seek medical attention if symptoms persist after the restraints are removed.

You'll also want to stay sober, keep any necessary release tools (including safety shears if you're using rope) within reach, and never leave a restrained partner unattended, even for a minute.

If someone wants to stop for any reason, release them immediately. “Don’t persuade them to continue and don’t make them explain themselves while they’re still tied up,” says Opel.

Consent is ongoing, even after the cuffs go on, and agreeing to try bondage once doesn't mean either of you is obligated to do it again.

Not everything that can be used as a restraint should be. Ideally, you want something that's comfortable against the skin, won't tighten unexpectedly, and can be removed quickly.

“I’d choose purpose-made soft or padded cuffs, Velcro or other quick-release restraints, or bondage tape designed to stick to itself rather than skin,” says Opel. If you're shopping in person, take the opportunity to feel the materials, check the sizing, and familiarize yourself with how the restraints fasten and release.

If it's rope bondage you're interested in, Moronta notes that materials like jute, hemp, cotton, and nylon vary in texture and how they feel against the skin. Try handling a few varieties during a bondage workshop before investing in your own rope.

As for household items? Scarves, bathrobe belts, and neckties might look relatively harmless, but they can slip or tighten unexpectedly. The experts advise against using metal handcuffs, zip ties, thin cords, hardware-store rope, or anything else that's rigid or difficult to remove. Duct tape and electrical tape are also a no-go.

For more beginner-friendly options, check out our guide to the best bondage restraints. You don't need to invest in an entire collection of BDSM accessories to figure out whether bondage is your thing.

#6826. Most Black Friday Sales Are Fake. These Ones Aren’t.

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

The Internet is a deep, dark place this week, but we found where the deals are worth it.

How do you even define a good deal anymore? The whole point of Black Friday was for retailers to make us wake up at the crack of dawn the day after Thanksgiving, wait in line, and then fight someone over a TV that was 50 percent off at Sears or Best Buy. How did they do that? They would sell a few products (doorbusters) at a loss just to physically bring people into the store. Those deals were good, and everything else, which you would buy because you were already there, was where the money was made.

That is now a thing of the past. Lines and physical altercations aside, in the past 20 years there has been a real swing in the favor of big retailers. First, we created Cyber Monday (though most people do their Black Friday shopping online already). Then the deals started a week earlier. Now, they last all month. And instead of having door busters to get you in the door, retailers just have very aggressive online marketing programs. In fact, it turns out that most Black Friday deals aren’t even deals at all. In a recent study, it was found that one in three Amazon Black Friday deals provided no true savings at all—prices were marked up earlier in the year, only to be brought back down to a standard retail value. The big retailers like Amazon and Walmart are the most to blame for these tricky strategies, but you should still be judicious when looking at any so-called Black Friday sales.

The good news? Black Friday is still filled with great deals—you just have to know where to look and what to expect. A lot of big wins revolve around private sales at more niche, direct-to-consumer stores. For example, Filson, one of our favorite outerwear brands, is having a 25-percent-off sale for Black Friday. That’s not the 75-percent-off you might have wanted, and there are other times that Filson goes 25-percent off. But the best strategy these days is to think about holiday shopping: Just buy the things you already would, but do it while they’re on sale now.

You should be especially skeptical of tech products. The increase in all tech prices has made it easy for those brands to push a 10-percent-off sale when products were 10-percent-off the current price. This is the sort of stuff we’ve been watching as the sales roll around. Based on this and years of covering sales and knowing what’s good and what’s not, we determined these are the best deals of the weekend. These are the deals our editors think are actually worth shopping this Black Friday.

Mr. Porter has an absolute goldmine of a sale. Like sure, you can grab this Brunello Cucinelli Jacket for $6,500 at 50 percent off. But it’s also filled with basics from brands like On that rarely go on sale.

Fortela is our favorite luxury westernwear brand with Italian design sensibilities. If you pay full price, you get every dollars’ worth in quality and concept. But shopping its archive sale and saving 50 percent? That’s highway robbery.

A cashmere-blend overcoat for 30 percent off is a real steal. Use code BLACKFRIDAY before it sells out.

A few days ago, the Samsung Frame Pro was 50 percent off. That deal was real, and it sold out. Today the Hisense Art TV (which we’re fans of) is 50-percent off. These deals vary daily, but today, this is the one we’d buy.

Dyson deals are confusing as fuck. You need to be knowledgeable about the model you’re buying into, and here that number matters. You will be able to find models like the V8 and the V10 for super cheap this week—but that’s because those models are old and outdated. Right now, the best and newest Dyson cordless vacuum is the V16—with all the bells and whistles, it retails at $1,100, but it’s $200 off right now.

But as someone who has used every Dyson, I know the V12 is a damn good model. And while it isn’t the newest, it still has lots of the same features as newer models and will last you years. So the fact that it’s on sale for $400 this weekend makes it a truly good deal. Also, I can’t find this deal on Amazon. For the best deals from Dyson, I would always check its actual site.

As previously mentioned, we love that many of Filson’s jackets are 25 percent off this week. This is a good example of when a brand just wants to participate in a sale, so they’re willing to mark down popular items. This jacket is so good our commerce editor Luke Guillory endorsed it last week, calling it the best $250 jacket. Guess what? Now it’s only $187. We know for a fact that this deal won’t last past Black Friday.

It’s expensive, yes, but Begg x Co. is one of the best cashmere brands anywhere in the world. $500 off a new cashmere sweater is something that doesn’t happen until the end of the season. But if you buy it now, you still have six good months of wear to get in.

Water filtration has become very expensive, especially when it comes to reverse osmosis and a countertop version that looks sleek. We have been recommending this one for over a year at $500, so the fact that it’s $150 off for once makes it a pretty good deal.

Furniture on sale is a whole category we can’t ignore. Furniture markups are a real thing, and a lot of it has to do with quality and materials. Marble is overpriced for sure, but good quality marble is worth it. We love Soho Home’s marble, and this dining table has been one of its most popular pieces for a while. Getting it for almost $3,000 off when you’re not a member is a big deal.

If you’re on the home redo kick, then a brand like Le Maé, which is offering some of its best wood pieces at 50-percent off, is a great place to start. Made with high quality materials and oak, this is one of those furniture pieces you will own forever.

If you’re a camo guy or do any non-deal hunting, then you know that Tom Beckbe jackets never go on sale—but this is your lucky week.

#6818. The Coolest Fashion Hub of the ’00s Was in a SoHo Basement

A new book captures the It girl scene at 163 Mercer Street

Back when Marc Jacobs was dressing the coolest girls of the aughts, retail wunderkind Robert Rich was his secret weapon. Not unlike Truman Capote and his "swans," Rich welcomed friends such as Kate Moss, Selma Blair, Sofia Coppola, Maya Rudolph, Natasha Lyonne, Parker Posey, and Winona Ryder to his basement office in the brand’s downtown flagship store, documenting fittings and gab sessions with a Polaroid camera. Now, 163 Mercer, a new book from IDEA named for the store’s address, shares stories and photographs of fashion’s golden years just before digital changed everything.

Rich's first book, Winona, made with Francesca Sorrenti, debuted in 2023 after he spotted merchandise on IDEA’s Instagram feed emblazoned with the name “Winona.” "I reached out and asked if they wanted to do a Winona Polaroid book, and they immediately replied, 'Yes!'" he recalled over Zoom. It sold out on day one, and a second printing followed the next year. The experience left him wanting more creative outlets.

163 Mercer is “directed” by Zoe Cassavetes, the director, screenwriter, and actress, who was the sales director of the nearby Mercer Hotel in the ’90s. She met Rich when Jacobs and Marc Jacobs International president Robert Duffy sent her to the store to pick out a thank-you gift for her professional hospitality at the Mercer Hotel, where Jacobs often stayed.

The duo, who are so close that they still speak on the phone every day, began brainstorming a project. "I had the photos of all the other girls, so I knew I wanted to do a book with those pictures," Rich said. They considered wallpaper based on the wall collage or a podcast featuring a different one of the girls per episode, but Cassavetes's film background, including her 2007 directorial debut Broken English, made her the perfect book creative partner. IDEA said yes again.

They worked at Cassavetes’s Los Angeles apartment, laying out images on her oversized office table. "It's a lot like writing a script, which is why I say I ‘directed’ the book; putting together the layout was like making a movie," she said. Rich occasionally asked her to add an edited image, and she agreed. "We have similar tastes, and we were open to each other's opinions. He has a cool eye," she added.

Their bond developed when Cassavetes worked down the street. "My title at the Mercer was director of sales, but I was really a VIP manager. I had a basement office, too," she recalled. Before New York's indoor smoking ban in 2003, the two took cigarette breaks indoors. "The logistics helped our friendship, hanging out in each other's offices smoking and having tea."

The book features images of regular visitors plus some who came once or twice, and the women graciously cataloged their memories for it. Don't expect captions throughout; it reads in parts like an IYKYK story asking viewers to figure out who is in the photo. "We didn't caption every Polaroid; they weren't like social media posts," Rich explained.

Nostalgia for an era before our feeds made the post-Covid years the perfect time for Rich to revisit his mementos. The book should appeal to members of Gen Z who are wondering what they missed before social media, and those in Gen X who are longing for a time that felt authentic, rather than conceived in a marketing strategy.

Trust bound everyone involved. Rich knew Moss previously, and Cassavetes knew Sofia and Ryder; Rich met the others on the job. Ryder came into the shop independently, and Rich professed his love of Girl, Interrupted. “’That's a girl's movie,’ she said, and I said, ‘I'm a girl's movie guy,’” Rich recalled. Ryder's infamous 2001 shoplifting case led to her starring in the brand's spring 2003 campaign, appearing on its "Protect the Skin You're In" T-shirts and wearing Marc Jacobs to court.

"Selma didn't know the others,” Rich said. “We hit it off when she tried on the Courrèges–inspired collection. I took Polaroids, sent some to Marc, and kept others. She kept coming in. I introduced her to Kate, Missy, and Frankie Rayder, all of them.”

The mood differed from today's brand-celebrity ecosystem of mutual monetary gain. "It was unpretentious; no one was there to get paid. We were hanging out and having fun. That was the Marc Jacobs spirit: more artsy, less corporate. It was a perfect zeitgeist moment," Cassavetes said.

Case in point: Rich met Hilary Swank before her Oscar win for Boys Don't Cry. "She would come to the store, and I would dress her up for all the pre-Oscar award shows and events. I put her in a tiered ruffle sundress with a beachy vibe for the Independent Spirit Award in 2000," he recalled.

Impromptu gatherings were plentiful. Once, Moss, Ryder, and Patric Reeves ended up in the office together. "I stocked my fridge with Sofia champagne cans. They were small but potent," Rich said with a chuckle. An image in the book documents the mini party. Though Polaroids waned in popularity after the brand declared bankruptcy and digital cameras and camera phones arrived, Rich kept a stockpile he used until 2015.

"Sometimes I wouldn't even recognize Winona because she had a new role, hair color, or style," he said. "But I met all the boyfriends, watched them get married, pregnant, have babies, and divorce."

Getting It girls to wear Marc Jacobs was simple. "Marc's clothes were unbelievable; you didn't have to beg them," said Rich, adding that the store's cool yet friendly vibe helped. "I was a big fan of Marc's, and that radiated to everyone I hired," including bartenders, who made great sales associates because "they knew how to talk to people." A generous clothing allowance, four outfits a season instead of uniforms, fueled employee enthusiasm.

Cassavetes remembers Rich's relaxed styling approach. "He made sure the girls didn't wear the same thing." Rich credits his former boss. "Marc liked everybody's take on his clothes. Winona would change the buttons or redo straps; he loved it."

Costume designer June Ambrose's favorite memories include discovering hidden treasures in the basement. "Robert has an incredible eye and instinctively knew what I needed; I could trust him. He understood the woman, the attitude, and the personality behind the clothes," she wrote in an email. "He made me fall in love with Marc Jacobs."

Rich also gave his editor and stylist friends early access to sample sales.

His Marc Jacobs career began when Joe Zee took him to his first runway show for the brand. "I was blown away and marched backstage and asked Marc for a job," Rich said. In 1999, he became store manager, eventually rising to vice president of public relations for retail stores during his tenure.

Before 163 Mercer became the Marc Jacobs store in 1997, it was once the Tony Shafrazi Gallery, which propelled the careers of Francis Bacon, David LaChapelle, and Keith Haring, for whom Rich once worked. "There was nothing in SoHo; Marc could have picked any space. There was good energy there. Tony would stop in and regret having given the space up," Rich said, noting Jacobs kicked off SoHo’s current designer shopping enclave.

"The store was so laid-back and a fun, creative safe space. It was also the center of the downtown fashion world at that time," Cassavetes added.

Rich hints that a third book would move away from SoHo. "We wouldn't just be in the office. Maybe it would be pictures from everywhere."

#6815. Curtain Bangs Are an Elegant, Low-Maintenance Style for Mature Hair: How to Wear It Now

Timeless and face-framing, this is the easiest way to update your haircut

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

From Sabrina Carpenter to Dakota Johnson, curtain bangs were among the most fawned-over hairstyles in the past few years. It’s not surprising; they flatter all face shapes and offer the face-framing effect of a fringe without the harshness (or any awkward growing-out stage) of a full, blunt chop.

Curtain bangs are also versatile at any age, and the cut has recently stepped into the spotlight as one of the most flattering styles for mature lengths. Penélope Cruz’s recent red-carpet appearance makes a convincing case for the look.

"Curtain bangs are one of the most flattering fringe options for mature hair because they soften the face rather than dominate it," explains hairdresser David Cassidy from Hove's Palette & Bristle. "They frame the cheekbones, draw attention to the eyes, and create movement around the front of the hair, which instantly feels more youthful."

Unlike a blunt fringe, he adds that curtain bangs blend into the rest of the haircut, creating an elegant, modern look with just the right amount of youthfulness.

Here, he explains how to get the perfect curtain fringe for mature hair this winter, along with key styling pointers.

As with any bangs cut, an expert eye and professional hand are key to achieving a look that suits your face shape.

"The key with curtain bangs on mature hair is softness and proportion," says Cassidy. "You want them to start no shorter than the cheekbone and taper gently into the length. Anything too short or too heavy can feel aging."

He also emphasizes texture; a slightly broken-up finish keeps them from looking flat and gives a more relaxed, lived-in effect.

"Before committing to curtain bangs, think about your natural hair texture and growth pattern," he adds. "Cowlicks, partings, and how your hair falls when it air-dries all matter. A good stylist will tailor the fringe to work with your hair, not against it. Curtain bangs are versatile. When done well, they grow out seamlessly and can be worn parted, swept back, or tucked away."

Before you veer away from your signature everyday style, consider how much extra styling time a new fringe might require.

"Curtain bangs are surprisingly low-maintenance if they’re cut properly," says Cassidy. "A medium round brush or even a large Velcro roller at the front while the hair cools will give that soft sweep away from the face."

He recommends styling your curtain bangs with the hair dryer angled side to side rather than straight down. "It creates lift without stiffness and keeps your bangs looking light and flattering."

In the world that Riordan has created, demigods roam the Earth in modern times. For the most part, they’re indistinguishable from regular kids. Some of them, like Percy Jackson himself, don’t even know that their parents are literally figures from Greek and Roman mythology. Since there are so many of those centuries-old tales, Riordan has been able to turn them into a ton of young adult adventures.

In the first book, Percy Jackson learns that he’s a demigod and enrolls at Camp Half-Blood. He meets Annabeth Chase and Grover Underwood, and the three of them go on a quest to find Zeus’ lightning bolt.

This time, the teenage demigods go looking for the Golden Fleece. They’re joined by Tyson, Percy’s brother who happens to be a cyclops.

In the third book, which happens to be the basis for the current season of the Disney+ series, the group expands and they go on a rescue mission. For who exactly? You’re going to have to read to find out!

Camp Half-Blood is under attack (again), and our heroes enter the mythical Labyrinth to save it from invading forces.

In the (original) grand finale, the fight moves from Camp Half-Blood to Manhattan.

Fifteen years later, Riordan returned to his original hero with a duology about Percy’s last year in school. This means quests and college applications.

The final (unless there’s more) book is set at Halloween as he pet sits for Hecate. Should be easy!

But wait, there’s more! Riordan has dozens of other stories, long and short, in this universe. Here’s enough to get you started:

This is a series about a group of seven demigods who embark on a quest together.

This series is, like it says on the tin, about Apollo.

Nico also appears in Heroes of Olympus. This continues his story.

This series is set in the same universe, but all about Egyptian mythology.

These short stories are Percy Jackson and Kane sibling crossovers.

This trilogy is about Annabeth’s cousin and his dealings in Norse mythology.

The most recent book, co-written by Annabelle Oh, has a female protagonist: Katie Kim, daughter of Ares. It will get a sequel called The Rite of Aphrodite in March 2027.
