#6739. Speculoos Scents Are the Cozy Perfume Trend Taking Over Winter

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Just as fragrance notes make up a perfume’s composition, fragrance families can also encompass their own layers of niche categories. Case in point: speculoos scents. Consider this emerging perfume profile an offspring of the beloved gourmand family. Gourmands home in on different kinds of sweet notes, whether it’s fruity, creamy, or, in the case of speculoos, reminiscent of freshly baked treats. Jeniece Trizzino, VP of Innovation and Physical Product at Scentbird and Drift, explains why this emerging category feels so seasonally appropriate and how to add them to your current scent library.

Like any gourmand, the note is built as an accord, a blend of materials your nose reads as one smell. “Ethyl maltol gives the burnt sugar. Vanillin gives the vanilla. Tonka bean adds a soft, hay-like warmth. The spices do the rest. Woods, patchouli, or musk sit underneath, so it smells like a perfume and not a dessert,” she notes.

Much like traditional gourmands, speculoos are built on familiar sweet cues: vanilla, caramel, chocolate, cream, and fruit. “Think cocoa with caramel and condensed milk. It’s creamy and comforting, and it leans toward dessert,” says Trizzino. A speculoos scent is sweet too, but it’s more spice-forward and toasted. The main difference is that speculoos scents lead with cinnamon, nutmeg, and cardamom. The addition of burnt sugar and browned butter allows it to smell baked, not syrupy. “You still get the comfort, with more going on. It can add complexity, not just more sweetness,” she adds.

Speculoos scents are carving out a place in fragrance as traditional gourmands evolve. “The very literal vanilla, caramel, and dessert scents can feel predictable now,” Trizzino points out. “The move is toward bitter, savory, and smoky contrasts. Traditional gourmands aren’t going away, but speculoos is one way to keep the comfort and add depth.”

Key notes: speculoos (cinnamon, cardamom), vanilla, sandalwood

Mancera’s Amore Caffè moves speculoos to the café. It’s built like an affogato. Black coffee and amaretto open it, then vanilla ice cream with a hint of speculoos, over vanilla, brown sugar, and grey amber.

Key notes: black coffee, amaretto liquor, vanilla ice cream, speculoos, vanilla pods, brown sugar, grey amber

Across its library, Kayali has nailed gourmand scents. What puts Freedom Musk Latte in this new category is its creamy, cozy, latte-inspired notes of cinnamon, chocolate musk, and café latte, punctuated with a burst of mandarin and pink pepper.

Key Notes: bergamot, café latte, chocolate musk

Key notes: cinnamon, coffee, cocoa, vanilla, musk

Jousset Parfums’ Mascarpone & Speculoos goes all the way to dessert. Mascarpone, butter, and whiskey open it. Coffee, cinnamon, cream and caramel follow, then vanilla, sugar and biscuit. It’s creamy, rich and unapologetically gourmand.

Key notes: butter, mascarpone, whisky, black coffee, caramel, cinnamon, cream, biscuit, sugar, vanilla

What makes these scents so seasonally appropriate is that winter is when people reach for scents that feel warm, comforting, and a little enveloping. Speculoos does all three. “The baking spices bring warmth. The toasted sugar and biscuit notes bring a familiar kind of comfort. It has the appeal of a favorite winter drink or something baking at home, but you can wear it,” says Trizzino.

Winter perfume has a reputation for being sweet and heavy. In contrast, speculoos is sweet, but the spice keeps it from being just sugar. “You get the comfort without the weight. And it travels. A recognizable food scent works in candles, diffusers, body care, and perfume, and it makes an easy gift.”

Although there’s already a lot of depth, speculoos scents are also layerable. “I actually think layering is where speculoos gets really interesting. It has enough warmth and sweetness to work as a base, but it’s also distinctive enough to change the personality of another fragrance.”

Trizzino says the best pairings depend on what you want to bring out of it:

For darker layering: woods and amber add depth. Cedar, sandalwood, amber, and vetiver balance the sweetness and make speculoos feel warmer and more sophisticated. Smoke, rum, and leather take it darker still. Tobacco, incense, rum, and leather add depth and make it a rich, comforting gourmand.

For richer layering: coffee and other gourmand notes lean into the dessert quality. Vanilla, tonka, chocolate, milky notes, and coffee make it indulgent. Baked fruit makes it seasonal. Apple, pear, or dates sit naturally with the toffee, vanilla, and baking spices of a winter gourmand.

For lighter layering: florals soften the spice. Jasmine, rose, and orange blossom add a more unexpected dimension and keep it from feeling too heavy. Citrus adds contrast. Bergamot, mandarin, and orange cut through the sweetness and give the scent a brighter opening. And a soft skin musk makes it more intimate. It can take speculoos from something that smells like a bakery to something warm and personal on skin.

Trizzino’s layering advice is to start with the fragrance you want to be most prominent and build around it. “You don’t need two scents that smell exactly alike. Sometimes the best combinations come from contrast. A simple way to start is with a familiar base like vanilla or sandalwood, then add one contrasting accent: fruit for a brighter blend, smoke or rum for a darker one. You can layer across formats too, with a perfume over a bodycare product,” she explains.

Speculoos doesn’t have to smell like dessert. It can smell like spice, warmth, woods, or skin. That’s what makes it fun to wear.

#6734. The Scoop with Kolor’s Taro Horiuchi: On His Zara Collab

Welcome to the Scoop: a weekly email series in which I quiz fashion insiders on the stories of the week. This will be a way for the Vogue Business community to synthesize and reflect on the latest headlines and get a little inside scoop every Friday.

This week’s guest is Taro Horiuchi, who took over the creative direction of Japanese brand Kolor from its founder Junichi Abe, a couple of years ago. Before that, Taro was running his namesake womenswear label, which he launched after moving to France in 2010, as well as a menswear line called TH Product, founded in 2018 (the two merged when he took over Kolor in 2025).

Before all that, Taro studied photography at London’s Kingston University and fashion design at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp, alongside Demna and Glenn Martens, who were in the year above and below, respectively. The thread that seems to bind Taro’s work together is turning basic garments on their heads, which is also what he sought to do in his most recent collaboration with a little conglomerate called Zara. I called him up to discuss that and more.

On December 3, we will be launching a collaboration with Zara. We are hosting a pop-up in Tokyo on December 2, and the global launch will be the following day. It’s the first global collaboration we’ve announced since I took over as creative director in 2025, so I feel honored to be in this position. The collection will span womenswear, menswear, and childrenswear. It’s the first time Kolor is making kids’ clothing, so that was an interesting challenge for us.

Shots from the Kolor x Zara campaign. It’s the brand’s first global collaboration since Horiuchi took over as creative director from founder Junichi Abe in 2025.

What was it like designing children’s clothes then?

The core challenge for us in this project was expressing the brand without the high pricing and intricate details. We wanted to make good, interesting clothes regardless of whether it was for children or adults. However, there are constraints when it comes to making clothes for children, both in terms of the textiles you can use and because the accessories and the parts on the clothing are very small. That was definitely a learning experience for us, which we took on happily.

Can you tell me a little bit about the collection? What was the inspiration behind it?

So the theme for this project is “World Uniform”. It’s something we do at Kolor: take something basic and turn it into something a little different. Fans of Kolor are always on the cutting edge of fashion, and they are always seeking something new. But those who shop at Zara are looking for clothes for their daily lives. So our challenge was to find the perfect balance between familiar and inspirational.

Behind the scenes of the Kolor x Zara campaign shoot. The collection’s theme, “World Uniform”, reflects Kolor’s habit of taking basic garments and making them “a little different”.

For sure, there are those who go to Zara for basics, but I’d argue that’s changing because of all the luxury brand collaborations Zara orchestrates, including the one with Kolor.

One thing that really stood out to me through this experience was the very high quality of fabrics and operations that Zara offers. My family and friends wear a lot of Zara, though I personally haven’t, so I wasn’t aware of the way they work. But the whole process was very inspirational to me. Both the product quality and the speed of responding were quite remarkable.

I remember when Zara launched in Greece; I was about 8 or 9. My mother was delighted because she could buy cheap but nice clothes for us. I still have some of those sweaters from 30 years ago, and my son wears them now. Has it been fun to work with Zara’s manufacturing resources?

For sure. When it comes to any collaboration, it doesn’t make sense for me to make anything you can make alone. I am very happy to say we managed to realize something that Kolor couldn’t have made on its own, and I believe Zara feels the same way about us.

A look from Kolor x Zara, which launches globally on December 3 after a pop-up in Tokyo on December 2.

You’ve taken over Kolor from its founder. It feels like a tough gig to follow a founder who is still involved and alive. But if we look at people like Julian Klausner at Dries Van Noten and Haider Ackermann at Tom Ford, maybe that’s part of the success recipe? How do you work with Junichi Abe, and is there a lot of pressure to match him?

I’ll answer your second question about pressure first. Of course, I feel the pressure, and I also respect Abe-san incredibly. Whether it’s a recipe for success, I’m not sure yet. What I can say is that the core value and DNA of a fashion brand aren’t something you can build in one day. It takes time. All I can do is what Abe-san told me to do at the very beginning of my time at Kolor: “Don’t repeat what I could. Just make Kolor unique to you,” he said.

There are quite a few open positions at the big luxury houses at the moment, and we expect them to be filled any day now. Does the constant change-up in creative directors affect the way you and other designers work or view the industry?

Things change much faster than when I started in fashion around maybe 2005. As I was saying earlier, building a brand takes time because it needs to have a culture and a philosophy. The compatibility of the brand and the designer is very important too in all that. In that sense, speedy changes are not good because they don’t allow the two to get to know each other.

Kolor x Zara. Horiuchi says the collaboration let him make something Kolor “couldn’t have made on its own”, thanks to Zara’s fabrics and production speed.

Applications for the 2027 LVMH prize are now open. You won the Diesel Award at ITS 20 years ago. How necessary are those awards and prizes to young designers?

I graduated from the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp in 2007, and I am still so thankful to Barbara (Franchin, founder and director of ITS) and Renzo (Rosso, founder of Diesel and founder and chairman of OTB) for the opportunity. Looking back now, this was a big turning point in my career. It wasn’t so much about winning the award, but more about the people I met. Demna was in the year above me at Antwerp, and together we organized an exhibition about Japan. At the Diesel award, I met Matthieu Blazy, who is now at Chanel. So, for me, those prizes and competitions are meaningful because of the communities they draw together. If you want to tell what the future of the industry will be in 20 years, you should look at who is entering those competitions now.

But I have a concern about the future of the industry. When I was a student, the tuition fees for Antwerp were around €1,000 per year. Now, for non-EEA students, it’s between €13,000 and €25,000. The people who can’t afford such high tuition will not be entering the fashion industry. Demna wouldn’t have been at Antwerp if the tuition was any more expensive. So maybe, one suggestion for the organizations that support those awards would be to focus more on scholarships and grants.

#6732. Jaime Ray Newman Thinks Season 2 of The Hunting Wives Is “Shakespearean”

Bazaar speaks with the actress in an exclusive interview to discuss the finale of The Hunting Wives season 2

In the first season of Netflix’s erotic melodrama The Hunting Wives, desire drives most, if not all, of Callie’s decisions—and indiscretions. Her unyielding loyalty to Maple Brook’s conniving diva, the formidable Margo Banks (Malin Akerman), springs from a delusional, obsessive, unrequited love—a love worth spilling blood over. This ardent personality is exactly what first attracted Jaime Ray Newman to the role.

“The first thing that struck me about Callie, when I auditioned for the part, is that she is a woman who yearns,” the actress tells Bazaar about her sharp-tongued character ahead of The Hunting Wives season two release. “This is a woman who deeply wants what she cannot have and maybe will never be able to have because of where she was born. We’re all victims of time and place. There’s so much that she wants that she cannot and may never have.”

The Hunting Wives, like Callie’s yearning, focuses mostly on Margo, the salacious wife of the richest man in town, Jed (Dermot Mulroney). Much of the first season’s conflict stems from Margo’s extramarital affairs with both 18-year-old Brad (George Ferreira) and Massachusetts transplant Sophie O’Neil (Brittany Snow). Then, the murder of a teenage girl rattles the tiny Texas town, and the gossip and backstabbing that follow are what both pushes Callie away and brings her back to Margo’s side in a triumphant, bloody ending. This valiant act revives her romance with Margo and also lands her a reality TV show, Married Justice, with her husband, Sheriff Jonny (Branton Box). “Season 1 ends on a high for Callie,” Newman says. “She’s just defended her woman, and Nancy Grace told her, ‘You’re a star.’ There’s no place but up from here. Callie ends season 1, thinking, ‘The world is my oyster,’ literally.”

In season 2, The Hunting Wives supercharges its soap-operatic storytelling, with much of the tragedy circling Callie’s character, a role Newman doubled down on for these eight episodes. “I find this to be Shakespearean in many ways,” Newman says. “It’s like a Greek tragedy, high drama.” This season, Callie’s arc is defined by utter heartbreak, as she finally confronts Margot’s true, evil, manipulative side and falls in love with a newcomer to Maple Brook, Nadia (Kim Patula), Married Justice’s producer. An effective tragedy depends on someone having something substantial to lose.

Bazaar spoke with Newman about Callie’s central role in the second season of The Hunting Wives, the tragic final two episodes, and how she believes her character is gearing up for revenge in season 3. Spoilers ahead!

I’m not a reality-TV-show watcher, but when I figured out we were doing this, I did a deep dive. For the photo shoot, I probably had 50 photos of these women from the Real Housewives in my trailer: how they posed, what they did with their lips, what they did with their hands, where their breasts were. My trailer was plastered with [their photos] and also Kristi Noem. We copied Kristi’s wig, and I studied her make-up. She’s in baseball hats and tactical gear. We stole a lot of ideas from her belts. May her career rest in peace, but she was a real North Star.

Margo gives Callie the greatest gift in saying, “You’re not my person; you need to move on.” She’s very clear about that. There’s the scene when I pull up in my truck, and I realize she left my romantic dinner I made for her and went to be with Sophie. Callie is devastated by it, but very soon after, this wonderful door of Nadia opens.

Kim had a really tall order, and it’s just become a hit with all these characters that have [gotten big enough to be parodied] on SNL, for God’s sake. To come and fill those shoes and find her little corner of this universe, I give her so much credit because she didn’t push and didn’t try to overwhelm anyone. It’s a very natural reaction to come on set and feel like you have to prove yourself. Kim is such a good actress that she leaned back rather than leaned forward. She made us come to her, and you can feel that in her performance. She’s so good. Isn’t she amazing? I loved working with her. Every time there was a Callie and Nadia scene, every day was a little different. She and I would rehearse on our off days. We’d run lines together, go to the gym together, work out together. We became really good friends. I didn’t know she was going to be killed because I didn’t get all the episodes. Early on, like in season 1, we got all the episodes. We walked into season 1 knowing everything, whereas in season 2, they came out in real time. But I had a hunch that happiness doesn’t last for very long in Maple Brook. Callie’s a little too happy here. Rebecca Cutter is going to rip that from her clutches very soon.

In the bar scene when Nadia tells me that she’s gay. I remember there were a bunch of takes that we did where I could barely even say the word lesbian. It could not exit my mouth. I don’t think they used any of those takes. I don’t think Callie had ever seen someone living a life she probably would want for herself. You wanting to be an actor as a child and having a real talent and propensity for it, but your family saying, “No, you have to be a pharmacist.” You [can] go about your whole life only thinking there’s one way, in one direction, and when you’re 40, you meet someone who actually was able to do that and did have a family that was supportive, and Callie sees these parallel lives. That’s what she sees in Nadia.

I was so devastated when I saw that Nadia was killed. I couldn’t believe it because I didn’t know. How can you do that to me?! I was so upset for Callie. What’s interesting is that when I watched the whole thing—they sent it to us a couple of months ago—in the final scene where I’m shooting at the Married Justice poster, I wasn’t shooting at that in real life. Rebecca had the idea to superimpose it, and I’m shooting Margo in the head.

We played it a bunch of ways. We did it one where Callie was 100 percent certain, I’m seeking justice. She made up her mind. We shot one one-take where I’m totally conflicted, and I’m crying. Actually, we put black eye makeup on to copy Nadia. We took black eyeliner and circled my eyes, and I had black makeup tears streaming down my face. We did one where I decided, “Fuck it, I’m going to suppress everything that I know is right and I’m going with Jonny to Austin.” So I didn’t know what would end up there.

My impression from that is Callie is going to go full force for revenge. How that plays into season 3, I don’t know. But how can she not? She’s a woman who has morals and values. She was on a TV show called Married Justice! She’s not going to abandon justice now that her show’s been canceled.

Who hasn’t had a moment where you tell your partner, “I did that,” and you’re like, “Oh my God, are they still going to love me?” That’s what that moment was, because she knows those photos can unlock and really take Margo down, but it’s also showing a side of Callie that’s very unattractive. She was under a spell—in the cult of Margo, which a lot of us join. She needed to believe that she could show these photos and take the risk that Nadia might think she’s too fucking batshit. She does it to serve justice.

Before we started shooting season 1, Rebecca Cutter, our showrunner, said, “Callie and Jonny probably have the best marriage on the show. I don’t think they are beards. I think they really, really love each other, but they can’t fully fulfill each other.” Also, he’s trapped. God bless Branton. I love acting with him, and he’s really a cowboy. He’s from Texas, and he’s a full foot taller than me. It’s great casting. A relationship is about understanding. What those rules are is made up by those two people, so who am I to judge their relationship? We all enter into a pact when you commit yourself to someone else. Callie’s makes me a little sad that she could be able to live a better life without so many secrets, but these are the circumstances she was born into.

We’re all speaking in code for much of this season. We say things through daggers in our eyes that we can’t say in public. Margo has caused nothing but grief for Callie, but she can’t quit her. She can’t escape the web that this woman weaves. Who better to do it with than the magnificent Malin Akerman? Callie goes from someone who thinks that Margo is the love of her life to Margo being the devil. I don’t know about season 3, but I don’t think Callie will rest until she gets justice.

#6731. The 40+ Best Black Friday Clothing Deals 2026

The gravy-soaked grub will settle soon enough, but you finally let the Black Friday clothing deals wash over your comatose self. And it’s not just the usual suspects like Banana Republic, Abercrombie, and J.Crew either. Though, yes, they've all been on sale since the beginning of the week and will continue to be on sale through the weekend. Aside from them, a gang of our favorite independent boutiques like Lost & Found, Haven, and Mr Porter also have a heap of discounted goods on taste-making labels like Auralee, Our Legacy, and Ssstein.

So whether you're shopping for your loved ones (remember, the holidays are here sooner than you think), or treating yourself to a nice end-of-year bonus (even if your job won't), this is the spot to be. Here are some of our favorite deals from around the web.

Abercrombie doesn’t have any specific promotions that are live at the moment, but the sale section was recently stuffed with some ideal fall building blocks—most notably some baggy cords—that will make a refresh as easy and affordable as you’d ever hoped it could be.

Rollnecks are perfect for adding a little spice to your outfit without going full turtle.

While your upper half is enjoying lambswool sweaters and puffy down coats, your lower half deserves something a little more sumptuous than denim during the cold season.

Few sweaters can strike a balance between tough, cozy, and downright fun like a rugby can.

Printed bouclé and fleece jackets are a hot commodity this season and this one from The Moose is completely dialed in.

Banana Republic has been on a heater recently, and the perfectly-curated Archive Reissue collection is leading the charge this season. It should also be noted that anything on the site that is on sale also gets an additional 20% off.

A tweed jacket like this is the perfect piece to dress up an outfit without taking it too seriously. Try it with some faded jeans and a polo or some cords and a cashmere sweater for an ace holiday fit.

Don’t tell anyone at Gap that Black Friday is a ways off, because there are a ridiculous number of in-season pieces up to 50%—sweaters, flannels, cords, jeans, jackets, and more—and it feels like raising too much awareness to that might cause some reconsideration and none of us want that.

Thanks to its thick-gauge yarns, shaker knit sweaters like this one are great for adding some texture without overheating.

Not everyone has access or the means to shop at an esoteric denim boutique, but most folks can walk into Gap and buy this classic trucker which puts Japanese denim brands on notice.

Haven isn’t promoting a sale anywhere on the site and you might have to dig a little bit depending what size you wear, but if you’re looking for some of the sickest IYKYK brands on the planet at insane discounts, there aren’t many places I’d rather start.

Especially in places with milder climates, overshirts are indispensable.

OG Japanese streetwear label Neighborhood is slept on these days, which means more for you and me.

Let's hear it for the dudes who aren't afraid of a weird hat.

Haven's moda operandi is to take an existing form and make everything about it better—this BDU-style jacket included.

If you’re not familiar with Huckberry, they preside over one of most thoughtfully curated assortments of menswear, footwear and gear anywhere, whether that’s IRL or URL.

Most black holes are mysterious physics phenomena where nothing can escape, not even light. This black hole keeps all your stuff together in one neat pack.

Under no circumstances will you regret treating yourself to a discounted Wythe flannel.

For reasons both indiscernible and inconsequential Timex's first mechanical release in over 30 years is under $200.

Nearly all of J.Crew’s spring-summer collection is on sale at the moment, over 300 pieces up to 40% off—including a whole bunch of heat-beating shirting, lightweight pants, archive classics and basically anything else you’d want to be on sale.

Is it really winter without a fun Fair Isle sweater? (No!)

Raglan sleeves, patch pockets, and a heavyweight wool. Enough said.

With a little bit of your T-shirt peeking out from under, a V-neck sweater like this is a chic way to throw in some layering and depth into an otherwise plain outfit.

Your thin socks aren't gonna cut it going into the freezing months.

The first name in denim has a pretty nifty “buy two, get 30% off” promotion going on site-wide, so if you’re searching for some jeans, you might just want to buy a couple pairs. (Or maybe a trucker. Or sherpa-lined trucker. You’re in charge.)

I might say that the Type II is the best iteration of the trucker jacket. Even better if you can get it in jet black for a steal.

Is it a coincidence that the Levi's western shirt is also a certified classic? No.

The more relaxed sibling silhouette to the famed 501, the Levi's 505 fit features a slightly more forgiving fit with a flattering straight-leg cut.

Primo for layering over a hefty hoodie and some busted work pants.

Diving into Lost & Found’s sale section is one of the more enjoyable shopping experiences one can have online right now: the selection is great, the brand list is a top-five worldwide and there’s plenty of inventory, which puts it in stark contrast with some of the less rewarding sale sections.

Post O'alls is one of those IYKYK Japanese brands that goes unnoticed by most (except you, because we're telling you).

Step out of your plain white tee comfort zone.

Skinny jeans may be coming back, but they have to go through this big badass painter pant first.

Menswear darling Auralee has the boys in a chokehold and if you're not seeing it in this beautiful garment-dyed coat, then that's okay—nobody's perfect.

One of the most quietly great, easy-to-wear brands in the game recently reloaded the sale section, and basically no category was left unturned. Of particular note, are the killer sweatshirts currently available with a healthy discount applied.

Thermals are a styling cheat code that works for everyone, thanks to their insulating waffle-knit texture. Layer this under your favorite band tee and thank us later.

Depending on the weather, you might only need a shirt or you might really need a jacket. With this, you don't have to think twice.

While folks are tripping over zip-ups and crewneck cardigans, we're still bullish on the classic V-neck cardigan.

Nothing like a huge coat to cover a multitude of fashion sins (like pajamas in public).

Mr Porter’s sale section is the kind you can lose an hour in without realizing it, even months after a seasonal sale has ended. Case in point: there’s roughly 500 pairs of shoes and 900 jackets on sale at this very moment, and while sizes might be hit and miss, the deals aren’t.

A nice sweater with nice texture and nice colors. What more do you need?

Roa's flagship hiking boot is as much of a mountain goat as it is a taste signifier.

The English tailoring wonks at Drake's also know how to make a damned fine workwear jacket.

While most pre-faded jeans look obviously manufactured, Ssstein manages to get the vintage, authentic fade spot on.

REI’s Deals section always lives up to the billing, but right now it’s about as good as it’s ever been. Hundreds of pieces from heavyweights like Arc’teryx, Patagonia, The North Face and more are discounted up to 50%, including plenty of winter-specific gear for anyone lacking in that department.

For the fitness nuts that still train outside in the winter, this is the hoodie you need.

One way to save on your heating bill? Turn off the heater and wear this instead.

Hopefully TikTok has moved on from taking showers with their Arc'teryx jackets on.

Danner's answer to Red Wing is a more affordable, equally handsome take on the work boot.

Todd Snyder presumably won’t be partaking in the Black Friday festivities this year—they announced a new sale structure a while back—but that doesn’t mean the already-on-sale fare doesn’t hold up to the promotions sure to fire up across the board.

For years, I would wear a shirt-jacket thing like this because it was handsome, comfy, and looked great with everything. Now, I'm coming back to my old uniform thanks to this luxe version from Todd Snyder.

Menswear isn't all jeans and double-knee work pants.

A buttery suede trucker is always an investment, but a $300 discount helps ease this jacket into "no-brainer" territory.

This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, a day after Thanksgiving. While that’s the official date, many retailers roll out deals throughout November. You can expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday.

Cyber Monday lands on November 30 this year, the Monday after Thanksgiving. Most brands keep the deals rolling through the week—but that doesn't mean a deal will last all day, so act fast.

Are clothing deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday both deliver a plethora of clothing deals, but they play a little differently. Big-name retailers and legacy brands usually kick things off on Black Friday, while smaller menswear boutiques tend to hold their fire until Cyber Monday. Expect solid discounts starting around 20% off—and keep your eyes peeled for the coveted sale-on-sale action that’s become the norm in recent years.

#6729. The Best Japanese Restaurants in London, From Omakase Counters to Neighborhood Gems

Finding good Japanese food in London hasn’t always been the easiest task, given the city’s abundance of mediocre sushi takeaway spots and gaudy central London restaurants serving sub-par fish dressed up with too many bells and whistles. (No piece of sushi has ever needed gold leaf so liberally applied.) Historically, to eat well, you’ve had to splurge: it isn’t cheap, after all, to source top-quality fish in the British capital, and it’s still worth saving your pennies for a blowout meal at one of the city’s top omakase counters, such as Sushi Kanesaka or Sushi Tetsu.

But in truth, you don’t need to break the bank to eat Japanese food well in London: just take the well-priced lunch set menu at Kiku Mayfair, or the reliably fresh sushi at any Eat Tokyo outpost, or the excellent quality-to-price ratio at Bond Street institution Chisou. (Its former location next to the old Condé Nast offices on Hanover Square led it to be nicknamed the “Vogue canteen.”) And that’s without mentioning beloved neighborhood spots like Uchi Hackney or Jin Kichi in Hampstead.

From exclusive six-seat counters to beloved West End izakayas, here is our definitive guide to the Japanese restaurants in London that are truly worth the hype.

Located within the ritzy 45 Park Lane hotel, this Michelin-starred, omakase-only destination with 13 seats is as atmospheric a sushi experience as you’ll find anywhere in London. Step through the discreet noren curtain that marks the entrance, and you’ll feel as if you entered a portal straight to Kyoto, with the gently lit interiors—all hinoki wood, lime plaster walls, and intricate kumiko lattice work—serving as a delicate backdrop for the equally delicate flight of dishes that follows. Helmed by legendary chef Shinji Kanesaka, the 13-seat restaurant offers a masterclass in traditional Edomae-style omakase using an impressive array of locally sourced ingredients: a silky pot of chawanmushi topped with the briny sweetness of fresh Cornish crab; marbled, melt-in-your-mouth fatty tuna nigiri with perfectly seasoned rice sourced from Japan’s Yamagata Prefecture; a Scottish lobster presented on a board then whizzed up into shatteringly crisp morsels of tempura. With a price tag of £420 per person, it isn’t for the faint of heart—but for those seeking true perfection, it’s London’s ultimate bucket-list sushi destination. —Liam Hess

A true Mayfair stalwart, Kiku has been serving the neighborhood since 1978, making it one of the oldest Japanese restaurants in the city—and unlike some of its flashier neighboring sushi restaurants, Kiku’s vibe is one of calm, quiet elegance. It’s the place to go for a consistently excellent, no-frills sushi experience where the quality of the fish speaks for itself, whether it’s the salmon and tuna in a classic sashimi set, or rare delicacies like Hokkaido sea urchin and sweet prawn served on perfectly seasoned rice. The tempura here is world-class, with a light, lace-like batter, and the £40 lunchtime set menu—which consists of yakitori, tempura, sushi, miso soup, and a dessert—is one of the best deals in central London. The ultimate seal of approval? It’s a favorite spot among the staff at the nearby Japanese Embassy on Piccadilly. —L.H.

This low-key but stylish joint, which opened in 2024 in a bijou shopfront on Brewer Street, is the brainchild of chef Takamasa Mogi—also the founder of popular Mayfair spot Cubé—and serves up astonishingly good sushi to the 10 seats that surround its subdued but stylish hinoki wood counter. (Soho regulars will remember the building’s former life as a manga store and karaoke bar—it turns out there’s still a karaoke room downstairs if your omakase dinner ends up getting a little raucous.) I was especially impressed by the creative but not overdone nigiri, including smoky slivers of seared Korean turbot and Spanish tuna with Oscietra caviar, served atop pillowy beds of red vinegar-seasoned rice. Given the quality, it’s excellent value too: the lunchtime menu offers salad, seven pieces of omakase nigiri, and dessert for £51.80, while the dinner menu of two appetizers, nine pieces of omakase nigiri, a temaki roll, and dessert comes to £89. (They also do a well-priced pre-theater menu if you’re planning to catch a West End show.) —L.H.

Under former Noma sommelier Yuki Kaneko’s ownership, Yuki Bar has transcended East London’s small plates and orange wine scene. Within the low-lit, 20-cover spot soundtracked by disco J-pop, dishes riff on French and Nordic classics with Japanese inflections, like a sesame-studded take on oeufs mayonnaise, embracing home-style cooking and a choose-your-own-adventure menu of “snacks, littles, and larges.” A few portions of house-made potato crisps with sansho pepper and grilled onigiri kick the evening off, while rotating mains have included an aromatic chicken hot pot and blushing strips of beef tataki silken with soy sauce and mustard. Go with a group, be greedy, and get a few bottles recommended by Kaneko. —Anna Cafolla

Mayfair isn’t exactly short on high-end sushi counters, so it takes serious pedigree to make a splashy entrance here. One of the few people capable of that is Shogo Amamoto, the Fukuoka-born chef behind Taipei’s two-Michelin-starred Sushi Amamoto—a reservation so notoriously tough to secure that die-hard sushi-heads are known to plan trips to Taiwan around it. (Sushi mastery clearly runs in the family: his brother, Masamichi, helms Tokyo’s cult-favorite Higashiazabu Amamoto.) Chef Shogo’s London outpost forgoes the usual Mayfair glitz in favor of a serene, minimalist room centered around a pale hinoki wood counter and bespoke Japanese ceramics, and the focus lies firmly in classic Edomae culinary craft. Dishes feature top-tier seafood flown in from Tokyo’s Toyosu Market alongside standout European catches—translucent slices of French wild seabass sashimi with shiso flower and ponzu, a sweet seared Orkney scallop wrapped in crisp nori, or rich, smoky nodoguro whose skin crackles straight off the grill—and warm, perfectly seasoned rice. It’s purist without feeling oppressively solemn—and one of the freshest (in every sense) new additions to London’s luxury sushi roster. —L.H.

One of London’s sexiest counter seats (and that’s saying something), Ushio arrives from Fukuoka, on Japan’s Kyushu island. Its first European location, Ushio serves A5 wagyu omakase style (no sushi here!), specifically akami wagyu that has been imported from Japan. It’s leaner and higher in protein, with a taste that will unfurl across an incisive multi-course menu of wagyu every which way. You’ll get a card that tells you which prime cut of beef you’re eating with every course, and it’s certainly a journey. Some are barely kissed by the grill, others draped in a rich sukiyaki marinade or glazed in their signature tare sauce. A trio of tenderloin, tongue, and kurimi are delicately salted and presented gloriously as is. (My tip? Say yes to the extra curry course! If it wasn’t so sophisticated in there, I would be licking the bowl. Add the sake pairing and enjoy your time with the very charming sommelier too.) Finish with a (meatless, but still mighty) matcha choux puff. In a quiet, darkened corridor of Fitzrovia, the minimal interiors are stunning and sleek, just like the Fukuoka flagship, built around wood and stone with Ko-Imari porcelains and hand-built ceramics by Taeko Kajihara. And everyone who works there just seems cool! A spot that lingers long on the palate. —A.C.

Tucked behind a bright white storefront in Clerkenwell, this seven-person omakase experience is among the city’s toughest reservations to secure. Husband-and-wife duo Harumi and Toru Takahashi are behind the operation (the latter being the chef), both of whom are famously warm and welcoming, fostering a convivial atmosphere versus the buttoned-up formality of traditional omakase settings. The seasonal menu relies on what is strongest in the market that day, but expect sushi so fresh it melts in your mouth and impeccable sake pairings. The restaurant sits along Jerusalem Passage, an 18th-century path to the priory of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem, which later transformed into a pedestrian walkway linking St John’s Square to Aylesbury Street. —Nicole Kliest

If you’re craving sushi but aren’t in the mood for a formal omakase environment, Uchi Hackney achieves an exceptional balance. This ultra-cozy spot in a residential area of Hackney leans on traditional Japanese design motifs (linen, ceramics, wood), and even encourages guests to kick off their shoes and slip into a pair of provided slippers. The restaurant began as a delivery service in 2015 and now offers a high-quality menu in its brick-and-mortar location, serving both brunch and dinner. As for the dishes, expect a variety of hot favorites such as grilled pork belly skewers and lightly deep-fried tofu, and savor the selection of fresh sushi and sake to round out the experience. (An aside: Uchi Hackney’s intimate ambience makes for the perfect date night locale.) —N.K.

Set on the ninth-floor Liverpool Street branch of Los Mochis, arriving at Luna Omakase comes with a delightful sense of ceremony. As the evening begins, you’ll be guided with your group from the bar along a nondescript corridor to a set of sliding doors that are opened—with plenty of theatrical flourish—to reveal the 12-seater dining room, where a sculptural timber counter is lit with a lunar glow against a backdrop of glittering skyline views of the City. Over the course of 12 seasonal plates, the vibe is lively and conversational, as the sushi masters hand each pristine slice of aged fish—think melt-in-your-mouth otoro tartare with Oscietra caviar served with a cloud of smoke, or juicy king crab leg nigiri with feathery shavings of yuzu—and artfully balance traditional technique and off-the-cuff flourishes throughout the meal. (If you fancy it, you can also make the evening more spirited—quite literally—courtesy of the tightly curated list of rare sakes and Japanese whiskies that the team is more than happy to geek out over, and that will serve as an instant conversation starter with your fellow sushi obsessives.) It’s intimate and undeniably stylish, but free of the stuffiness that can make your typical high-end omakase experience feel a little intimidating. —L.H.

In operation for nearly 30 years, this beloved sushi institution now operates across eight outposts in London (plus six in Tokyo). For those who favor great value and generous portion sizes, this restaurant chain consistently gets top marks. Choose from a menu of sushi, sashimi, nigiri, chirashi, unagi, or opt for a bento box to get the full experience. Their latest creation worth dining out for? Wagyu with black tobiko (or a ‘sushi taco’, as it’s so nicknamed). —N.K.

This Japanese udon noodle bar opened its doors in Soho back in 2010 and has since expanded to three popular London locations, plus a shop offering provisions such as chilli oil and jars of Fukujinzuke. The original location is worth a visit for the freshly made noodles and dashi alone, but don’t sleep on the weekly blackboard specials either (previous highlights include grilled corn with miso butter and fried whitebait with shibazuke cucumber). Koya Soho is walk-ins only and is open from breakfast through to dinner. —N.K.

This is where you go when you want authentic Japanese food and a killer sake selection, all in a calm, relaxed setting. Chisou’s two central London locations—Mayfair and Knightsbridge—treat guests to seasonally changing dishes and a menu of wow-worthy raw fish, with the option to sit at a sushi bar or at an intimate table. And back to the sake for a moment: Chisou prides itself on having one of the largest menus around, with experts on hand to suggest pairings and special events like sake and British cheese pairing classes led by specialists. —N.K.

A charming, intimate spot tucked away on New Quebec Street in Marylebone, Roketsu recently relaunched as a rare example in London of kappo-style dining, where the chefs will whip up a customized set menu based on a conversation about your preferences at the beginning of the meal. The team of chefs here take a creative approach to classic Japanese cuisine, folding in a handful of French flourishes: most notably, perhaps, with one of the restaurant’s signature dishes, an opening bite of a crisp wafer filled with 10-day miso-marinated foie gras. (Other highlights included Cornish cod with a vibrant nori sauce, and flame-grilled wagyu beef with yuzu oroshi for a clean, citrus-forward finish.) With an open kitchen behind a hinoki wood counter, Roketsu is an elevated, classically Japanese dining experience—but it also comes with an element of choose-your-own-adventure fun that makes it feel genuinely unique. —L.H.

If you’re seeking a quirkier spin on omakase dining, head over to Notting Hill, where you’ll find the six-seat Juno hidden in a speakeasy-like space at the back of Los Mochis, the popular neighborhood Mexican-Japanese restaurant on Uxbridge St. The dining room’s delightfully funky, “Tokyo-meets-Tulum” decor—bamboo, seagrass, high-gloss wallpaper—should serve as an initial clue for what to expect here: the textures and flavors of Japanese cuisine are lent a fresh twist courtesy of a bold, Mexican-inspired toolkit of spices, acids, and smoke. (Think chutoro spiked with a sharp kick of fermented jalapeño, or red bream brushed with lime aioli and topped with a sprinkle of crushed-up Oaxacan flying ant for a surprisingly delicious note of nutty earthiness.) Bring your friends and make it a party. —L.H.

There are few more scenic spots for lunchtime sushi in London than chef Endo Kazutoshi’s rooftop restaurant, which sits proudly above the Raffles London hotel at the Old War Office—and trades the monastic restraint of Endo’s Michelin-starred White City flagship for sweeping views over Horse Guards Parade. Grab an outdoor table and browse a menu that bridges Japanese precision with Mediterranean flourishes, the latter a direct nod to the years Kazutoshi spent cooking in Spain. Most of the dishes are built for sharing, so order generously: try the tuna tartare on miso brioche, the yellowfin tuna “chorizo” (its smoky, paprika-laced punch is balanced by pickled tsukemono and warm pita), or the charred, melt-in-the-mouth octopus with miso, fava beans, and asakura sansho—it’s all rather decadent, but somehow never overly heavy. Come for the pristine, perfectly seasoned nigiri; stay for the golden-hour sunset over the Neoclassical rooftops of this stately corner of central London. —L.H.

Many of the best Japanese restaurants fall into two categories: no-frills neighborhood ramen and udon spots, or the kind of hushed, six-seater omakase counters where you might be frowned at for asking for extra soy sauce. Aki London, tucked inside a soaring, Grade II-listed former bank on Cavendish Square, couldn’t be more different. Designed by Francis Sultana, the dining room is all about pure, flamboyant glamour—think fluted marble columns, soaring coffered ceilings, and plush velvet banquette seating. This isn’t a case of style over substance, however: The kitchen leans into farm-to-table Japanese cooking rooted in Kyoto traditions, ranging from crisp, featherlight tempura rock shrimp to delicate steamed-and-crisped wagyu gyoza, to smoky, tare-brushed chicken thigh skewers straight off the robata grill. Whether you’re coming for a leisurely lunch or a late-night dinner, make sure to check out the subterranean cocktail bar first for a round of yuzu-infused martinis. (Aki is best enjoyed in the company of a lively group.) —L.H.

A neighborhood restaurant in the truest sense, Jin Kichi’s cult following makes booking a table a competitive sport. This tiny, two-floor restaurant is cozy, often crowded, and wonderfully authentic. While the yakitori is a major draw, the sushi and sashimi are of a quality that rivals the city’s most expensive counters. #6727. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6725. 8 Best Body Trimmers for Manscaping With Ease in 2026

The best body trimmers for men are one of the most important grooming tools in your medicine cabinet. Whether you’re looking to trim your down-there hair, corral your pits, deforest your back, shave your ass, or all of the above, it’s good to know your options. And, because dealing with body hair doesn’t always mean shaving it all off, the best body trimmer for you is the one that gives you the results you want.

You might want a multi-purpose manscaper for hitting all points north, south, east, and chest. You might want a skin-so-smooth shaver that leaves you more hydrodynamic than an Olympic swimmer. You might need something that’s body-part specific. ("Best trimmer for balls" is a perennially popular search for a reason.) The point is: No two men will take the same path on their body hair journey. This is why we’ve done the work, testing every body hair trimmer we can get our hands on, and we've found the best body hair trimmers on the market for just about every guy who needs one.

Black Friday is here, and the deals are hitting fast. For the biggest and swerviest markdowns, editor favorites, and elite-level shopping intel, keep it locked on our roundup of the best Black Friday deals and best Black Friday clothing deals.

The Philips 7000 is a convincing way to clear some space in the bathroom cabinet. Its bundle pairs body combs for 3mm and 5mm trims with attachments for beard, nose, and ear hair. That gives it a broader role than a dedicated body shaver, particularly if you want to keep some length on your chest.

My usual Philips complaint applies – it still needs its own charging cable rather than the same USB-C charger that works with your iPhone. Depending on which bundle you pick up, you also might not have an “intimate comb” supplied with it, so I’d choose the Meridian Slimmer for a close trim below the belt.

Long-term testing notes: During three weeks with the 7000, it worked through my thick chest hair without pulling. Its slightly boxy handle was surprisingly comfortable around my underarms, with a textured grip that stayed secure at awkward angles. I also liked how well it handled facial hair, giving me a reason to keep one tool handy for several jobs. Esat Dedezade

While you might be able to get away with leaving your trimmer at home for a weekend by the shore, things have a way of unraveling fast over longer trips and vacations. For extended stays, you’ll want to pack a handy grooming companion to keep you tuned up from head to toe. The Lawn Mower 5.0 Ultra is designed to cross state lines and beyond: from the handy travel lock to keep the trimmer from powering on in your carry-on to the high-quality travel case to keep its attachments and charging cable organized.

The unique design of two adjustable length trimming guards allows each to be used to achieve three different lengths, which makes for easy transitioning and also saves space in the carry case. In our testing, the trimmer performed with reassuring power and accuracy. While 60 minutes is not the longest battery life, the trimmer’s constant RPM motor ensures the blade won’t slow down as battery levels dip. In any case, when it is time to charge, the Lawn Mower 5.0 Ultra supports USB-C and wireless charging. Adam Hurly

If you’re ballin’ on a budget, Remington’s All-in-One Groomer is a capable, familiar trimmer that shouldn’t set off any fraud alerts on your credit card. Out of the box, this lightweight grooming tool is comfortable to hold, and the blade head twists into place with a satisfying click. The trimmer’s three fixed guards offer a standard spread of lengths, ranging from 3–9mm; and, for anything in between or beyond, the adjustable comb guard unlocks 10 additional length settings between 2–20mm. We were particularly impressed by the adjustable guard, which proved to be a handy tool for safely fine-tuning short to medium-length body hair with confidence. With additional attachments including a nose and ear trimmer, as well as a refined detail trimmer, the All-in-One Groomer lives up to its name, providing full-body coverage at an affordable price. Adam Hurly

Won't settle for anything but the kind of hairless finish worthy of an Olympic swimmer? Philips' Body Groomer 5000 is the device pick up over a conventional trimmer. Its Triple Protect shaving system combines trimming and foil shaving, and there's also a separate trimmer head with adjustable combs covering 1–7mm. So you can leave some length on your chest or switch to the foil for a closer finish.

That head and comb arrangement differs from the British kit I reviewed, which had fixed guards and you’ll also need Philips’ own charging cable. It’s a familiar gripe when rival devices offer charging over UBS-C, but a small one next to how comfortably the shaving system worked for me.

Long-term testing notes: Over several weeks with the 5000, I used the cutters on either side of the foil to take down longer chest hair, then angled the foil against my skin to clear the stubble. Rushing through dense patches caused the occasional tug, but slowing down solved it. Below the belt, I got a smooth finish without cuts or irritation, and the light handle stayed comfortable through a longer session. All of which left me happy enough to put my wet razor away for a while. Esat Dedezade

Shaving your own back is a time-honored chore for the hairiest among us, and the Mangroomer Intellimax Pro brings a home-inventor level of crazy brilliance to a job that otherwise requires extreme contortions. You just unfold it, power it on, drop it over the first shoulder, and get to mowing. The trimming head doesn’t bite or leave marks, but will take hair down to the normal .5mm, while the foil-head shaver attachment will get you smooth-skinned (for maybe a day or two). You can even adjust the length of the Mangroomer’s handle for taller torsos or to get better angles on tricky spots.

It was a lifesaver for me when I was single (before I could sweetly ask my partner to do the job)—and so simple that shaving my back almost became fun. I would use it directly in the shower, making for easy cleanup. (Though never with the shower running; it's waterproof, but I didn't want the handle getting slippery enough that I’d drop it.) I never had any issues with nicking or razor burn with the Intellimax Pro’s main trimming head, though it was trickier to get a uniform shave using the foil shaving head. Frankly, it was easier to just use the .5mm trimming head every day if I wanted to stay stubble-free. Adam Hurly

The Slimmer’s compact head is its main attraction. There’s less machine to maneuver around tight spots, with two combs for leaving some length and a light for a better view – it stays off when you first switch the device on, and another press of the power button brings it into play. USB-C charging also saves you packing another cable. I just wish Meridian had included a pouch – with a trimmer this small and two loose combs, it feels like an obvious omission.

Its two combs cover 1.6mm or 4mm of hair length, so there’s some choice when you don’t want to take everything off. If you prefer longer chest hair, the longer guards on Meridian's Original model make more sense. Still, the Slimmer is the device I’d pick when close control over a blade matters most.

Long-term testing notes: I relied on the Slimmer for around a month on my chest and below the belt. The narrow head made awkward spots easier to navigate, and it cut through thick hair without pulling or nicking me. Without a comb, it left a hint of stubble I was happy with, although the Philips 5000’s foil gets smoother results. As for its ergonomics? The soft, grippy handle was comfortable, and the hinged blade made it easy to rinse out trapped hair. Esat Dedezade

The OneBlade arrived on the scene years back as a hybrid between an electric trimmer/shaver and a manual razor, with replaceable cartridges ensuring you always had the sharpest cutting surface. The Intimate SkinProtect version steps up the game with coated teeth that protect against bites without compromising on stubble maintenance. For truly sensitive areas, I’d still recommend using the low-profile buffer guard to prevent friction or snips. And if you’re already a OneBlade owner, you can just buy the Intimate SkinProtect cartridges, and swap them on when you start working below the neck.

Right out of the box, the Black Ops inspires confidence with its well-weighted, stainless-steel build—wrapped in a grippy rubber handle to eliminate any chance of a slip. While it may sound like something you’d download for your PS5, the Manscaper Black Ops isn’t playing any games when it comes to getting the job done. The trimmer arrives with eight guards ranging from 1.5–13 millimeters, as well as an adjustable guide comb to give you more options for your hair down there. And, like its amphibious namesake, the Manscaper Black Ops is fully waterproof.

We look for trimmers that can get through thick growth without pulling and are easy to control when we get to the awkward bits. We pay attention to how securely the guards fit, how comfortably the handle turns around the body, and how much work it takes to get a smooth finish. Cleaning, battery life, and charging matter, too, especially with a tool that may cover several grooming jobs.

Adam Hurly and Dean Stattmann bring their grooming reviews and health and wellness coverage to this guide, For this update, Esat Dedezade has also drawn on his body-groomer testing for British GQ. The entries identify whose findings support each recommendation, and advice from celebrity groomer Dan Perri helps explain what to look for and how to maintain the tools.

For a professional opinion on what to prioritize when buying an electric shaver or grooming kit, we sought out the expertise of celebrity groomer Dan Perri, who keeps A-list clients like Post Malone, Gerard Butler, and Brendan Fraser looking tidy. Here are the key attributes of a good body hair trimmer, says Perri:

“If you want the best performance out of your trimmer, keeping the blade clean and lubricated is key,” says Perri. “Oiling the trimmer every few weeks will keep the blade running smooth, prevent any pulling of the hair, and keep the blade temperature down.” He adds that most trimmers come with a small supply of mineral oil—use it. (Wahl sells a great 4-oz clipper oil for cheap, too.) Be sure to use a machine-safe disinfectant spray to help keep the blade sanitized, which will prevent breakouts, Perri adds.

Can you use a beard trimmer for manscaping?

Some beard trimmers are designed for use on the body, but only if they have attachments designed to keep skin from being pulled into the blade. Keep in mind that the ergonomics of a great beard trimmer doesn’t necessarily align with the ergonomics you’ll want for shaving body parts. You’ll have a harder time hitting hard to reach places, like the back. And beyond that, you’ll want to aggressively sanitize any trimming heads and guards that touch both your face and your… [looks down].

What is the best body hair trimmer for men?

We recommend the Philips Norelco All-in-One 7000 Series for most people who want to keep some length on their body hair. The 3mm and 5mm body combs let you choose how much to leave. For a smooth finish, go with the Body Groomer 5000 Series and its dedicated foil head.

Depends! If you want to be as smooth as an Olympic swimmer, you might want to shave every day. If that's too much of a hassle, doing it every two or three days can be sufficient to have you smooth without your stubble scratching up your shirts.

Do you find body hair unsightly? Then maybe you want to shave your body hair to give yourself a smoother appearance. The decision to trim body hair usually depends on what you or even your partner prefers. For professional sports, a hairless body might be preferred for an advantage, like for swimmers or wrestlers.

Is it better to trim body hair when it's wet or dry?

You can shave your hair whether it's wet or dry, but we prefer doing it on dry hair. Trimmers are able to more easily cut through the hair when it's dry, and you can get more even cuts if you're not going for a clean shave. (Though wet/dry trimmers are all over the market.)

Besides using non-skinsafe grooming electricals (we got you covered in that department), some common manscaping mishaps are the result of poor technique (shaving against the grain), not trimming on cleansed, exfoliated skin, and neglecting post-shaving moisturizing—especially if you have sensitive skin.

Razor burn is no joke. Preparing the skin, using proper shaving technique, and including lotions, moisturizers, and other skin car products into you grooming routine are all good ways to prevent razor burn.

Dan Perri is a celebrity groomer based between NYC, LA, and Florida. His A-list clients include Post Malone, Gerard Butler, and Brendan Fraser.

#6723. “I Don’t Care About the Pointed Foot or the High Leg”— Celia Rowlson-Hall Looks for Authenticity in Movement

The choreographer is taking on Spring Awakening’s Off-Broadway Revival

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

One evening in November, Celia Rowlson-Hall slipped into a conference room for a rare break. The choreographer has spent the past four weeks rehearsing a new Off-Broadway revival of Spring Awakening, directed by Tony winner Danya Taymor, and it’s the second day of tech week. She had been holed up in Studio Seaview’s adjacent theater, fine-tuning “The Bitch of Living,” an angsty number about wet dreams, busty piano teachers, and Nietzsche. Previews were set to begin in a little over a week, and Rowlson-Hall eagerly tucked into a takeout grain bowl, fueling up for her evening ahead.

Set in 19th-century Germany, Spring Awakening is about the turmoil of developing sexuality in teenagers in a society attempting to keep them in ignorance. In 2006, the playwright Steven Sater and the musician Duncan Sheik adapted it into a musical that won eight Tony Awards, including for choreographer Bill T. Jones, who translated rebellion and repression into a gestural vocabulary. That original production also launched a generation of musical theater stars, including Jonathan Groff, Lea Michele, and John Gallagher Jr. In this spirit, the production held an open audition that attracted 2,532 performers (two actors were cast from this process). Rowlson-Hall kept her eye out for those actors with a sense of grounded earthiness and truthful storytelling. “I’m always going to be looking out for authenticity and personality inside of movement,” she says. “I don't care about the pointed foot or the high leg; it's never interested me, even as a dancer. I've never understood dance for dance’s sake.”

Spring Awakening will mark Rowlson-Hall’s theatrical debut after nearly two decades of directing and choreographing for screen. Among her work are the scenes of ecstatic prayer in The Testament of Ann Lee and Aftersun’s devastating rave sequence (she also played the adult version of the lead character). Humorously, she recently appeared in The Drama as a dance teacher intent on perfection, a mentality that couldn’t be farther from Rowlson-Hall’s own intuitive and empathetic style.

With big blue eyes and a choppy mop of dark hair, Rowlson-Hall, 42, is expressive even when sequestered behind a conference room desk. She frequently puts her fork down to gesture, including when recalling a friend’s suggestion “that all artists have one or two rocks that they will turn over their entire lives.” Rolling a pair of invisible stones around in her palms, she names religion and femininity as her thematic preoccupations. “The impact of religion in the body, specifically the female body, and what femininity looks like as taught to me by my parents versus from society and my own experiences.” She laughs, adding, “As my other friend said, ‘Celia loves a repression era.’”

Like the characters in Spring Awakening, Rowlson-Hall grew up in a small, religious community. In her case, it was Urbanna, Virginia, population 492 as of 2020, in a Christian Scientist household. She started dancing at 5 and knew from a young age that she wanted to use movement to tell stories of her own. After studying at the North Carolina School of the Arts, Rowlson-Hall moved to New York in 2006, the same year Spring Awakening premiered. “I remember hearing about the show, but also being too poor to go,” she says.

Two years later, she was planning to start her own dance company when she was asked to choreograph a music video for MGMT. She immediately felt at home on a film set, and also appreciated that the medium offered a more enduring result than a concert dancen ephemeral live performance. “The forever part,” she says. “I needed it then in my life.” She continued working on music videos, commercials, and television, absorbing lessons on filmmaking along the way. After a series of movement-based feminist shorts, Rowlson-Hall used Kickstarter to finance her first feature, Ma (2015), in which she stars in the dialogue-free dance film as a modern-day Virgin Mary on a pilgrimage to Las Vegas.

Rowlson-Hall met her now-wife, director and showrunner Mia Lidofsky, while choreographing Girls’ acclaimed “Beach House” episode in 2013. Rowlson-Hall was in a heterosexual marriage at the time, and she describes coming out at 30 as “this incredible aha moment.” But then, “Shame came in and clamped me down. I stopped moving.” It was a confusing contrast: while experiencing a profound sense of freedom and selfhood, she became disconnected from her body for the first time. Rowlson-Hall is anxious to elaborate. “The impact of me coming out was very difficult on my family, they initially had a hard time accepting it,” she says. “Then my mom got very ill, and I put my life and body on pause because I was so scared for her.” From there followed a decade of extreme highs (falling in love, marriage, motherhood) and lows (divorce, several deaths including both parents). “There were a lot of roadblocks for me to be able to find physicality and movement again because I kept getting knocked down,” she says.

She credits Ann Lee with allowing her to feel that connection again. The writer and director, Mona Fastvold, is a close friend; the two met back in the day on Gossip Girl. Rowlson-Hall was eager to inhabit the 18th century visionary, an illiterate blacksmith's daughter who became the founder and leader of the Shakers. “As a kid, I used to love to pray, it was my favorite thing,” she says. “I really wanted to ask myself ‘what if I got to decide what prayer looks like?’” She could also relate to the Shakers’ use of dance as transcendence. “From when I was young, I always felt like I was needing to exorcise things out of my body that weren't mine,” Rowlson-Hall says. “So much of what I do is trying to clear out to actually understand who I am.” The viscera is not strictly a metaphor. “When I feel like I'm going to vomit, I know that I've tapped into the right thing,” she says. “I choreograph from there, and then I can't touch it again.” She makes a gagging sound. “And then it's out of my body.”

Rowlson-Hall returned to the stage last year with Sissy, a semi-autobiographical dance-theater piece reimagining the myth of Sisyphus as the struggles of a female artist tasked with caring for a young child and an ill father. “There's something about theater and motherhood that feel very aligned,” she says with a laugh. “It's all alive and happening in front of you, and you've got to love it and let it go. It journeys on without you, you actually have no control.” That said, she’s working on her next film, which she describes as “a time traveling love story of Eve and Lilith exiting the Garden of Eden” and spending lifetimes together and apart. “There they are again,” Rowlson-Hall says. “Those old stones.”

#6721. Elizabeth Debicki Is the Heart and Soul of 'Cliff Booth'

The following article contains minor spoilers for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

It might seem strange, the notion that people have been surprised to find that a David Fincher film, written by Quentin Tarantino and starring Brad Pitt, is “actually good.” But moviegoers had their fair share of reasons to be skeptical of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth: chief among them, that Tarantino was forcing a mind-melding of the auteurs that could prove disastrously incongruous simply because he didn’t want to blow his long-awaited 10th and final film on a sequel. The 10-film rule is, of course, completely self-imposed, a mandate Tarantino is stubbornly sticking to instead of realizing he can still employ strict curation and quality control without limiting his filmography to a perfect even number. But now that he’s actually, finally, on what will be his last movie (according to his rules), there’s this notion that he’s afraid to pull the trigger—which some believe he all but confirmed when, in 2023, he announced his 10th film would be called The Movie Critic, only to completely retract that a month later.

Two years later, Tarantino sat down as a guest on (what else?) The Church of Tarantino podcast, hosted by two QT superfans, which is actually a pretty fun listen in between all the excessive stanning. So quickly do they bring up QT10 that it’s obvious the director was anxious to set the record straight. Tarantino tells the hosts that TMC started as an exercise in attempting to write a compelling story about “the most boring” profession imaginable. Despite succeeding, he realized he wasn’t excited by it once the film entered pre-production. There was also a version of the story that he adapted into an eight-hour miniseries, until he realized he had no interest in the process of selling and making TV either.

It’s similar to the way he’s talked about what became Cliff Booth, which started as a novel before morphing into an unwieldy feature script until Pitt convinced him to let someone else take a crack at directing it, lest these titular misadventures go to waste. Watching the film last week, my ears perked up when, in the midst of being courted by Cliff, high-powered Hollywood agent Karen Crosby reveals she got her start in the industry as a… movie critic. She reflects back on her time writing about film derisively, describing the profession as one with a low barrier for entry.

Karen is instantly one of the most beguiling characters in a movie filled with colorful performances both big and small. Played by Elizabeth Debicki with an icy, over-it resolve, Karen’s nagging fascination with Cliff makes for what one critic aptly described as Tarantino’s best-written romance since Jackie Brown. Despite being the closest thing to a co-lead, you walk away from the film feeling like you haven’t seen nearly enough of her.

Later in the film, Debicki gets a showy, highlight reel-worthy monologue where Karen, instead of extolling the virtues of cinema as a former critic might, recites what’s apparently an infamous credo among her close friends: that film, while entertaining, hardly rises to the level of being true art. (This is much to the delight of one of her clients, A-list TV star Charlie Peters, played by Scott Caan.)

It was at this point that I was certain we were watching remixed and repurposed scenes from The Movie Critic—and that if Karen Crosby wasn’t the eponymous character, she was at the very least a gender-flipped version. In one of the only times Tarantino talked openly about his erstwhile film, he said it would be “based on a guy who really lived but was never really famous, and he used to write movie reviews for a porno rag.” Meanwhile, the internet ran with the idea that the film would actually be a not-so-thinly-veiled tribute to Pauline Kael. Karen, for what it’s worth, name-drops Kael when describing her past life.

That this is among the best scenes in the otherwise thoroughly enjoyable Further Mis-Adventures only underscores how silly Tarantino’s 10-film imposition is. Look, l I agree with him: as a logline, it hardly sounds exciting enough to be a career finale, but a Tarantino-directed version of the movie probably would’ve been a good time given how much the director clearly enjoys luxuriating in this world. He can write odes to ‘60s and ‘70s cinema in his sleep. But because it would be a retread with no 11th script to follow, it’ll never see the light of day.

Or will it? I hate to enable weird science, but The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth doesn’t simply work; it’s one of the best movies of the year. Can another director submit himself to Tarantino’s tone and vision the way Fincher does so gamely here? Would Fincher even want to do that again? Hard to say on both fronts, but if Tarantino is going to keep being precious about his next (last?) directorial outing, the least he could do is let someone else execute his other ideas before they start collecting dust. Even Tarantino’s B-Tier is still a great time at the movies.
