#6718. Vintage Watch Experts Break Down Their 6 Favorite Timepieces

This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

And another thing, a watch collector might say as they try to sell you on the virtues of the hobby, is that you can bring them anywhere. Unlike other high-value collectibles—cars or paintings, say—you can wear even the rarest of grail-worthy timepieces to, say, a dimly lit bar. Which is precisely where James Fisk—the photographer behind the images in the just-released Vintage Watches: The Modern Guide, written by the renowned dealers Eric Wind and Charlie Dunne—encountered one of the most historic tickers in the book.

Last September, Fisk was at the Waldorf Astoria in New York when he spotted a collector wearing the coveted 1940s Longines model known as the “Tre Tacche.” Watches are challenging subjects even in a photo studio, but Fisk was forced to stumble around the hotel bar looking for any slice of decent lighting to capture the Longines before it slipped through his fingers forever. Used to working on the fly, the photographer keeps 40 or so fabric swatches with him at all times, just in case he needs to lay a watch on top of one as a backdrop for an impromptu shoot.

“You meet someone who just happens to be wearing something really special on the wrist that day, and you have to just be ready for it,” Fisk tells me. It’s how many of the legendary vintage watches—mildly important subjects for a book on the topic—ended up in Wind and Dunne’s new tome.

The book is a comprehensive deep dive into the booming world of vintage watch collecting. Wind and Dunne take readers on a Jungle Cruise-style tour of this sometimes daunting hobby: On your left are the questions that all newcomers should know to ask before buying a vintage watch; on your right, you’ll find testimonies from famous collectors like David Chang, Ronny Chieng, and Daniel Dae Kim; straight ahead are dispatches on the most important brands, from Rolex to Piaget.

Vintage Watches: The Modern Guide is designed to be as welcoming and accessible as possible. While many watch volumes sell for hundreds of dollars, Dunne and Wind made it a point to price theirs at $60 (or $50 on Amazon right now). “A lot of people will be able to afford this book,” Dunne says. “And then, hopefully, they’ll aspire to get some of the watches in it and it’ll ignite their interest in the hobby.”

Below are Wind and Dunne’s favorite selections from the book, including one that the latter was most insistent on including to represent the more affordable side of the spectrum.

There may be two six-figure watches on the cover, but flip just a few pages into the book and you’ll find this delightful little example from Fortis. “I forced Eric to put that in,” Dunne jokes. “He said, ‘We're not putting that in—it's too cheap!” The watch sells for just a touch over $1,000, and this exact piece was in Wind’s collection for several years. He calls it a personal favorite from his years of collecting.

The Shipman might not be historically important or carry great provenance, but it serves an important dimension in the book as a representative for the many types of pieces that comprise a true collection. “Not only [does it show] the range of what is out there as far as exceptional watches at all price points, but also it's one of the most fun and quirky watches in the book,” Dunne says. “You want to have very, very serious watches in your collection, but you also want to have things that put a smile on your face at any price point.”

How do you choose the cover stars for a book about vintage watches? You start with the obvious: The Rolex “Paul Newman” Daytona (bottom) is the poster boy for vintage collecting. The famed Phillips auctioneer Aurel Bacs, who sold the actor’s personal version for a record $17.8 million, calls Newman wearing this special variant “the Adam and Eve moment in Rolex collecting.”

But the Daytona’s partner on the cover, the Audemars Piguet ref. 5516, is an unexpected choice that packs just as much historical heft. “This is one of the most important watches ever made, because of the leap year indicator” Wind says. “AP beat Patek by over 20 years to have a leap year indicator on the bottom. This and the Royal Oak are probably two of the greatest impacts on the Swiss watch industry.” Only nine were made, and Wind sold this example for $545,000 while he was at Christie’s in 2015. I love the specificity of the watch’s leap-year function, which only comes into play once every four years.

Wind and Dunne are longtime evangelists for the Seafarers that Heuer made for Abercrombie & Fitch in the late ’40s and early ’50s. This particular reference is modified to include a tide indicator at the 9 o’clock subdial, done up in extremely pretty tones of sandy tan and deep sea blue. The example featured in the book remains pristine—with a perfect eggshell-white dial—thanks to the original owner stuffing it in a drawer unworn for decades. The watch got to Wind by way of a friend, whom he sent to fetch it from a diner in the original owner’s home state of Arizona.

The watch that Fisk scrambled to shoot in a hotel bar was well worth the hustle. “Longines, in some sense, was Rolex before Rolex,” Wind says. The brand was “the tool watch manufacturer in the 1930s and 1940s, particularly with their Tre Tacche cases. Many of the great aviators and pioneers of the time wore Longines watches.” The model gets its nickname from the three notches on the caseback that helped watchmakers screw the case together tighter to prevent water and dust from getting inside.

This is a classic watch—a defining example of a dress model—done up with a particularly sleek dial. Patek Philippe made endless examples of the 96, allowing collectors to select their favorite flavor from the lot. Wind and Dunne sold this example but both wish they could have it back. “ I don't think it's coming to the light ever,” Dunne laments.

To capture the glossy black dial in the book, Fisk shot the watch at two different angles to mimic the experience of tilting it back and forth in your hands.

The very last watch added to the book was this version of the GMT-Master, one of the Crown’s most important models. The ref. 1675 isn’t the first GMT-Master that Rolex made, but it’s considered the platonic ideal visually and the most collectible among vintage watch lovers. Its predecessors featured troublesome bezels that were prone to cracking, as well as poisonous amounts of radium.

The 1675 was produced for just over 20 years, from 1959 to 1980. This one belongs to Fisk and was on his wrist when we met last week. “We got this right as the pages were printed,” Dunne says, “and we started yelling in emails [to the publisher] saying, ‘We have to stop everything. Put this page in there.’”

#6717. Sarah Pidgeon Ticks Off Two of Winter’s Biggest Outerwear Trends in One Viral Coat

It’s been a banner year for Sarah Pidgeon’s outerwear wardrobe. The actor, who made her debut on Vogue’s Best Dressed list this week, has spent much of 2026 investing in a really good collection of coats. And while playing Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy in Love Story has furnished Pidgeon with an extensive knowledge of the late fashion publicist’s preferred ’90s silhouettes, her own tastes are often a little more irreverent and varied.

Taking in a Knicks and Cavaliers game at Madison Square Garden in New York this week, Pidgeon ticked off two of the season’s biggest outerwear trends—animal print and flourishes of faux fur, as well as the sophisticated standing collar shape—in one covetable coat. The actor wore the Dolly Maxi by Carelli, an elongated iteration of the label’s cult jacket, with cream-and-black spotted, pony hair-effect fabric, a jaw-grazing collar, and fluffy chocolate-brown cuffs. Pidgeon let the coat do most of the talking, adding straight-leg blue jeans, pointy black boots, and her trusty black Balenciaga Le City bag, which she clutched under her arm.

Carelli is one of the runaway fashion success stories of 2026. Founded by Anna Carels in early 2025, the brand has amassed a celebrity clientele that includes Dua Lipa, Olivia Dean, and Peggy Gou, as well as legions of fans on TikTok. As Carels told British Vogue earlier this month, the original Dolly sold out in under an hour. The designer’s penchant for old-school glamour chimes with a broader appetite for rather louche, vintage-inflected outerwear: See Conner Ives’s decadent fur-trimmed creations and Charlotte Simone’s always sell-out fuzzy numbers, as well as the proliferation of vintage silk opera coats on everyone from Kendall Jenner to Hailey Bieber and Jennifer Lawrence. After several seasons of austere and minimalist coats, we’re all in the mood for something a little more flamboyant. (Vogue’s predictions for the hottest coats of the coldest months says just as much.)

Pidgeon is no stranger to the timeless pleasures of a leopard-print coat. During her Love Story press tour, the actor stepped out in Adam Lippes’s leopard chenille Margaux coat in a subtle nod to Bessette-Kennedy’s own affinity for animal print. She’s also made a habit of punctuating her more pared-back outfits with leopard-print accessories.

Elsewhere in her enviable outerwear rotation? A collarless leather trench from Aflalo, a sculptural peplum jacket from Celine, and the supple Prada leathers she sported during fashion month.

Working with stylist Emma Jade Morrison, Pidgeon has struck an interesting balance between the restraint that characterized CBK’s wardrobe and her own more adventurous inclinations. She has an eye for younger labels, too, and a knack for assimilating their more idiosyncratic designs into an otherwise unfussy wardrobe of great denim, white tees, and ’90s-coded accessories. The Carelli coat feels especially at home among them. Consider Sarah Pidgeon’s latest outing some inspiration: swap out that sensible black winter coat in favor of something with a little more personality. Match point!

#6713. Every David Fincher Killer, Definitively Ranked

David Fincher is a rare breed of chameleonic auteur. In the past 40 years, he's directed music videos, commercials, feature films, and television series, all of which keep garnering more cultural importance, either immediately or in retrospect (hey, look, David Fincher directed a 1987 video for a single from a random Philly bar rock band!) Fincher is known for his technical prowess, his “impossible eye,” and his pioneering mastery of digital technology. He’s made love letters to old Hollywood, ripped-from-the-headlines tech-industry autopsies that render depositions as white-knuckle suspense, and popcorn home-invasion flicks. He’s taken turns at IP-franchise stewardship, adapted bestselling airport paperbacks, and told the oddly touching story of a mild-mannered, even-tempered gentleman from New Orleans who ages backwards. But if Fincher has a career throughline, a raison d’etre, it’s his pursuit and depiction of killers—a focus made quite overt in The Killer, a fascinating and highly meta film which hits Netflix Friday after a limited theatrical run over the past two weeks.

In Fincher's films, killers—particularly serial killers—provide an extreme window into human nature. They are symptoms of a sick society, prophets, self-appointed Gods and monsters, blank canvases for us to project our conspiracies and insecurities onto, or would-be celebrities killing for attention from a sensation-hungry media that's all too happy to give it to them. In the pale light of day or the fluorescent light of a prison visiting area, they're often sad, awkward misfits who understand themselves and their actions even less than we do. But by necessity, they're also methodical people who must put a great deal of thought and care into their grisly work in order to continue working. In this way, Fincher sees them as the equivalent of process-mad directors, blocking their victims and staging their crime scenes before selling them to a confused but riveted public.

Time and time again, across his filmography, the image most associated with Fincher is the killer— or the hapless detectives pursuing them—shot from below, almost swallowed whole by a monochromatic backdrop that looms both far above and far behind them, dimly but immaculately lit, and bathed in shadow, inside Fincher's uncommonly steady, all-seeing and all-knowing frame. The killer’s maniacal focus, their certitude, is ours. The detective’s confusion—their understanding that they’re a step behind and a beat late, that they will never get the satisfying answers, the closure they’re looking for—is ours, too.

So for art, and for fun, let’s evaluate the many killers who've made Fincher's body of work as incredible and indelible as it is, based on a shifting, subjective equation of quality, efficacy, body count, and how they’re represented by the auteur himself.

Fight Club is a satire about bereft ineffectual masculinity, about neutered men crushed under Ikea catalogs, about eighth-grade-boy-level rebellion against materialism, capitalism, and every societal convention that places value on anything except chiseled abs, skinned knuckles, bullshit patter, and rugged individualism.

The “kill” here is committed by Edward Norton, as a character identified in the credits as “The Narrator” who murders Tyler Durden—his child, his liberator, his tormentor, and his imaginary friend—by, uh, shooting the side of his mouth, sort of? Somehow, the famously meticulous Fincher lands on a resolution that makes absolutely no sense according to the laws of physical interaction between The Narrator and Tyler Durden established within the rest of the film. Why does this apparition, who knows everything the narrator knows, and can punch The Narrator, can harm him physically without receiving the impact of those assaults, and can’t even be hit by The Narrator, die with his brains blown out as a result of his alter ego shooting off a chunk of his jaw? This is, hands down, the worst “kill” in the Fincher filmography.

22. The Random Guy Who Kills Madonna, “Bad Girl” (1993)

Fincher did his most important music video work for his muse and rumored paramour Madonna, who tapped him to direct videos for hits like “Vogue” and “Express Yourself.” But one of their less heralded collaborations was this bizarre minor work, a video (for a song from Erotica) that plays like a dumbed-down Wings of Desire. Madonna is a stressed-out high-achieving corporate type who unwinds by making bad and eventually fatal decisions. After her Bruno Ganz-like guardian angel (Christopher Walken) makes out with her, she pursues sex with a hookup who clearly intends to murder her. We only see the killer from Madonna's POV, and when he kills her it's presented as her choice, rather than the result of any kind of premeditated plot by the killer; he's more of a prop than a person.

21. Weyland-Yutani Employee, Alien3 (1992)

For a filmmaker who so regularly trades in death, Fincher has depicted shockingly few frivolous ones. Nearly every kill in his work is personal and meaningful. But this is an exception. Towards the end of Alien3 , a commando representing the wantonly evil corporation smokes Francis Aaron, one of the COs on the prison planet Ripley has crash-landed on. The scene underscores the cynical ruthlessness of the outfit, but ultimately it’s just a faceless grunt shooting a stranger.

20. The Security Guard, Fight Club (1999)

In the act of executing Operation Latte Thunder, an ingenious plan to weaponize a piece of corporate art mounted in an office park fountain to destroy a franchise coffee shop in the lobby of a nearby building, Robert Paulson (Meatloaf) is murdered by an extremely extra security guard, who shoots him in the head as he flees the scene of the crime. It’s another somewhat frivolous murder, but the fallout tells us a lot about Tyler Durden’s cult of personality and its effect on its dumbass followers.

19. Frank Underwood, House of Cards (2013-2018)

There are several killers from this groundbreaking, trashy Netflix politico soap you won’t see on this list. This is because the totality of Fincher’s involvement is unclear—he may have imprinted his filmic language on the entirety of the show's run, but he only directed the first two episodes (unlike Mindhunter, his second effort with Netflix, on which he directed seven of 19 episodes across two seasons.) But in the House of Cards pilot, in order to show us just what kind of devious, deliciously shitty archvillain Kevin Spacey's Francis Underwood is going to be, he gleefully, flagrantly bucks the old screenwriting maxim “Don't kill the dog”—and not for the first time—by having Frank strangle his pooch, which has been hit by a car.

The heroine of Aerosmith’s outlier conscious anthem reclaims her narrative by killing her rapist father. It’s an odd “message” song and an odd video, but both were groundbreaking and transgressive at the time. It’s a completely justified revenge killing that Fincher had to sell through suggestion to get played on MTV.

17. Lisbeth Salander, The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo (2011)

Lisbeth (Rooney Mara) slaps the shit out of Martin Vanger (Stellan Skarsgård) with a long iron, then chases him down on her motorcycle as he attempts to flee in a Range Rover, causing him to crash and burn. When she cocks a gun and asks Daniel Craig’s Mikael Blomkvist, “May I kill him?” before lighting out after Vanger, devoid of emotion, it’s the most badass moment of a very badass film.

Bald Sigourney Weaver kills the “Runner” xenomorph by setting off sprinklers after it jumps out of a river of molten lead, causing it to explode. Then—rather than allowing The Corporation to take a parasite chestburster out of her and potentially spare her life—she swan-dives backwards into the lead, killing herself and taking the alien with her—a sci-fi Joan of Arc.

15. Gottfried and Martin Vanger, The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo (2011)

Playing the role of a sicko pervert hiding in plain sight is a stretch for Skarsgård; Martin Vanger is a second-generation killer who shits on his dad for putting up rookie numbers and has a whole secret sex dungeon in his basement where he’s presumably killed dozens of women. Sadly, we must deduct points because Martin ends up dying as a result of overlong monologuing, like a 70s Bond villain.

14. (Tie) Monte Rissell, Rose Barnwright/Frank Janderman/Benjamin Barnwright, Jerry Brudos, Dennis Rader, Richard Speck, Darrell Gene Devier, David Berkowitz, William Pierce Jr., William Henry Hance, Elmer Wayne Henley Jr., Charles “Tex” Watson, Charles Manson*, Paul Bateson, Wayne Bertram Williams, Mindhunter (2017-2019)

David Fincher’s great Netflix series, a history of the FBI's Behavioral Science Unit, takes place mainly in the aftermath of its serial-killer subjects' various sprees, so we see few dead bodies onscreen. But as it turns out, talking to killers in quiet rooms and delving into their psyches is just as sensational and disturbing as the graphically depicted comic-book corpses in Se7en. The show is two Feds tearing the cover off America and discovering a teeming morass of perverts beneath the floorboards, up to their necks in muck. What we discover—in this crucial chapter of what feels like a career-long attempt by Fincher to unmake Se7en and its godlike antagonist—is that a lot of these killers are dull, impulsive, mentally-ill misfits and outcasts.

“To support devices," cheers Herman Mankiewicz, after delivering the first draft of his masterpiece, Citizen Kane. In the biopic written by Fincher’s father, booze is the fuel that allows the screenwriter to write, but kills his career one painful, impolitic-outburst-filled social interaction at a time, before it finally kills him, too. Alcohol is the lubricant that powers Mank’s genius, even as it obfuscates that genius and speeds his demise. The bottle both makes him and unmakes him, like Popeye if spinach destroyed his liver. It’s a self-inflicted slow killer, which makes its work all the more painful and tragic to witness.

12. (Tie) Raoul & Burnham, Panic Room (2002)

In Fincher’s masterful and inventive “conventional” thriller, Raoul (Dwight Yoakam) domes spoiled, insufferable, cornrowed Junior (Jared Leto) when he tries to walk away from the robbery they're pulling. Later, Burnham (Forest Whittaker) sacrifices himself and $22 million in bearer bonds to kill Raoul and save the day. Hard to say which is more satisfying.

11. Tobacco, American Cancer Society Commercial (1985)

The Big Bang of Fincher’s career, when he transitioned from Industrial Light & Magic cameraman and matte photographer to auteur. His first effort was this commercial, made for just $7,000, which several television stations banned because it was too graphic and disturbing. We have to side with the networks on this one—it’s a truly horrifying ad, a nightmare vision of the Starchild puppet from 2001 as a fetus double-fisting darts in the womb. But it’s an impressive work of visceral agitprop, one that had the potential to reconfigure the way we thought about this deadly but fairly common behavior in the 80s.

In Fincher’s latest, Michael Fassbender plays the unnamed, titular assassin in a procedural that’s all process. He's a classic Fincher protagonist, a type-A creature of habit and ritual. The wrinkle is he kind of sucks at his job—or at least, when we meet him, has reached a point where he’s no longer able to execute his work according to the dispassionate code he lives and works by.

So, yes, he’s obviously baited into killing John Doe, and basically gets his wife killed by being an idiot and giving his name to her killer in an angry impulsive rush when John Doe is right next to him pretending to be a nosy reporter, and by giving into his emotions and impulses he’s throwing his life and his career away—but Mills ranks this high because of Pitt's incredible work in the tortured moments before Mills fulfills John Doe's master plan. It's an all-time great performance that's seared into your brain forever after you've watched it once.

8. The Verdusco Brothers, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026)

Matt Groove and JB Tadena play Eddie and Fernando Verdusco, the gangster antagonists that walked directly out of Quentin Tarantino’s cinema-fried brain and into Fincher’s latest. The film has been sold as a play on a chatty Elmore Leonard crime story, but with touches like the Verduscos, it’s more like a muddy puddle of all different stripes of exploitation film, from noir to horror to splatter. The Verduscos are Filipino but present as Yakuza hitmen, with a dash of Mortal Kombat cartoonishness. It’s easy to give characters badass motherfucker names that insist upon themselves, with writers and directors who simply expect us to find them scary and cool with little to no proof besides a slow-mo entrance and a needle drop. But Tarantino and Fincher earn the mythology with a particularly terrifying and gnarly introductory home invasion murder (invoking Panic Room) of a family of four. Esmeralda, the rhino-killing war hammer brandished by Fernando, has the instant iconographic “weapon as characterization” power of which Tarantino’s longtime friend and collaborator Robert Rodriguez would be envious.

Alien3 is Fincher’s canon event; the formatively traumatic experience of tangling with a cynical studio on his first feature made him the director he became. Having the film taken away from him taught Fincher the importance of demanding complete creative control. So it’s either ironic or brilliant that in many ways, this Xenomorph is a metaphor for the director, an alien antagonist (with the characteristics of a rabid dog!) resisting a sinister corporation that wants to cage and exploit him for its own evil purposes.

6. Time, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (2008)

In a movie about a guy born as an old man who ages in reverse, a byproduct of his disease is Benjamin (Brad Pitt) must “blend in”, experiencing his childhood in an old folks home where death is routine. Benjamin Button lives outside of time, breaks the rules of time, and in the process explains the ravages of time. Throughout the film we watch everyone around Benjamin die: From war, from old age, from disease, and finally, from being born in reverse. It contains the most stunning and heartbreaking kills in Fincher’s filmography because they are not a product of a sicko's grand design, but simply nature taking its course, harrowing in its obvious, matter of fact inevitability.

The breakout star of Mindhunter, Edmund Kemper was the Co-Ed Killer—a hulking monster who killed many people and occasionally had sex with his victims' decapitated heads—and in the show, he’s the catalyst for the birth of the behavioral science unit. Cameron Britton plays Kemper as a verbose, precise, calmly menacing giant with thick frames and a trim mustache. He’s the most Fincheresque antagonist in the series. Kemper is lucid and clear-eyed, incisive, articulate, and occasionally even funny. Understanding what he’s done—and exactly why and how he did it— is critical to the protagonists' mission, and Kemper understands this, which makes him that much more terrifying.

Another meticulous, disciplined Fincher avatar who has checked every box and arranged for every contingency. Amazing Amy is a feminist archvillain exploiting misogyny to liberate herself from the American prison of marriage and the cool-girl wife’s role therein. She’s a deeply petty scorned woman of iron will, expert at manipulating the public, the authorities, staged crime scenes, and her husband.

3. Cliff Booth, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026)

In their fourth film together, Fincher and Pitt unlock their greatest character, which is doubly impressive when you consider that, the first time we met Booth, it earned Pitt his long-awaited Oscar. This version of Cliff Booth, nearly a decade older and mostly washed, is a more interesting character and one of Fincher’s greatest killers because he unlocks a darkness that is only hinted at in Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood. In that film, Cliff is an affable and doggedly loyal sidekick. When he kills (on screen), it’s self-defense, protecting his buddy from harm, and you can squint and think, “This just might be a roughneck, badass dude with a heart of gold.” In this installment, Cliff operates according to his personal moral compass, which in some cases involves premeditated, entirely avoidable, cold-blooded murder. He’s observing a uniquely American form of zen, existing in an overloaded sensory flow state on a spectrum that encompasses all manner of kinetic pleasure, remaining at ease and even-keeled whether he is bartending, Demolition Derby driving, getting slapped by a Goddess with frying pan hands, running a film projector at the New Bev, clutching an Old Chattanooga, or, of course, killing.

The film, and the killer, that has in many ways defined Fincher. Speaking to Esquire, before releasing Zodiac, the director said, “I don’t want to make a film serial killers masturbate to.” The line was an obvious dig at his own second feature, which is pure serial-killer porn and would set the template countless lesser movies would aspire to going forward. John Doe is a true mastermind who executes creative, horrific, gimmicky murders inspired by the Bible's deadly sins. But most importantly, he’s always a step ahead, always smarter than the cops coming after him, and his win at the end is absolute. Morgan Freeman’s terrified exclamation at the film's climax sums up the plot of the whole film: “John Doe has the upper hand!”

In Fincher’s masterpiece of form and statement, he’s at the height of his powers, revisiting the serial killer as a “celebrated” cultural figure and a malignant expression of society, and what he comes back with is maddening emptiness. Instead of a running inner monologue, we’re given nothing—not even the killer's identity (or identities.) The first half is a painstakingly made and researched film, scrubbed of all romance and sentimentality, that comes as close as fiction can to mimicking the endless, mundane texture of reality. Then, the killer dissolves.

To Fincher, the Zodiac Killer isn't a person, but an idea, an unanswered question, an unresolvable puzzle. Although different actors show up playing people who might be the culprit, the Zodiac haunts the film mostly as an absent menace. Conflicting motivations and theories are thrown at the viewer and it’s impossible to sift what circumstantial evidence is real from bullshit. Some characters favor one suspect, some another, nothing ever adds up, and no one is ever proven conclusively right or wrong. Years pass, people fall in and out of life, they succumb to their demons. Only devastating, lonely obsession remains.

#6710. Queen Letizia Makes the Case for a Two-Shoe Kind of Day

If you’ve ever peeked inside the capacious tote bag of a fashion editor or discerning corporate queen, you’ll know the merits of carrying a second pair of shoes. (Especially at this time of year, when a day at the office might segue into several festive engagements.) It seems that Queen Letizia of Spain is also well versed in the art of the midday shoe swap, albeit with a slightly more sophisticated, regal approach.

On Wednesday, the Spanish monarch joined King Felipe VI and the Austrian president and first lady, Alexander Van der Bellen and Doris Schmidauer, to inaugurate the Mariana of Austria exhibition at Madrid’s Museo Nacional del Prado, before hosting a luncheon at Zarzuela Palace. Rather than changing outfits between engagements, Letizia switched out her shoes to produce quite a different effect.

The queen opted for a burgundy pantsuit from Spanish label Bleis, comprising a single-breasted blazer and straight-leg pants, worn over a pink tie-neck blouse. She brought out the pink further by layering on a punchy, fuchsia Carolina Herrera felt coat that has been a firm favorite in her wardrobe for years.

She accessorized with a burgundy JW Pei Noor top-handle bag, pointed-toe Magrit kitten heels in a matching shade of leather, and zigzagging diamond earrings by Bárbara Goenaga, neatly rounding out her royal ensemble.

Come lunchtime, Letizia had traded her pointed pumps for a pair of pale pink patent Sézane Paula Babies: a rounded toe, double strap, and sturdy block heel shoe. The French label’s retro-inflected Mary Janes have become something of a wardrobe staple for the royal, who owns them in no fewer than five colorways. Her morning’s footwear emphasized the sharpness of her tailoring, while the second pair brought a sweeter sensibility to suiting.

Burgundy and pink proved itself a popular color combo on the fall 2026 runways, particularly at Chanel under Matthieu Blazy, with wider shades of red and pink at Celine. Queen Letizia has long had a knack for making the season’s more adventurous color trends work within the parameters of her royal wardrobe, too. Earlier this month, on a visit to Campus Diversia, she teamed a pair of navy corduroy pants with chocolate-brown outerwear and sturdy boots. Over the summer, she embraced yellow in a gathered Adolfo Domínguez dress flecked with other pastel shades. And who could forget her coronation weekend wardrobe all the way back 2023, when she went from a zesty green Victoria Beckham dress to a head-to-toe Barbie pink ensemble?

What compounds the Spanish royal’s elegant sense of style is that so much of it is defined by pieces she’s had for years, reconfigured according to her schedule or the prevailing fashion mood. With a swift change of shoes or a refreshed color combo, you needn’t have the resources of a royal wardrobe to pull it off.

#6708. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6706. 30 Nordstrom Black Friday 2026 Deals That Go Harder Than Expected

While we're all recovering from too much Thanksgiving turkey and sides, the Nordstrom Black Friday sale is looking like the perfect distraction from helping to figure out the seating plan for your sister's wedding next summer.

That’s because, as always, the famed department store is your ideal all-in-one stop for any style need—a dapper new suit, a pair of comfier kicks, some killer watches. But these days, it’s also the place to lock in your new skincare routine or find a scintillating cologne, not to mention a whole new kitchen full of Michelin-starred gear and practically a full-on home renovation with luxurious bedding and tasteful decor. All that and more are on offer for the Nordstrom Black Friday sale, and we’ve looked through the entire thing to surface some truly gloat-over-Christmas level deals.

Whether you need a new suit for the holidays, a pair of boots to get you through Snowmageddon, or a head-to-toe closet refresh, Nordstrom’s got it all discounted. That goes doubly for Veilance's incredible, rain-defying outerwear. We don’t expect that to last long.

Accessories are the bits and bobs that really make your outfits pop. Whether it’s the watch on your wrist, the beanie on your head, or the duffle you carry on your travels, no detail—or discount—is too small.

We think that some of the best things to buy at Nordstrom are shoes, suits, and grooming products. Nordstrom also has a surprisingly good amount of designer and niche brands on their roster—you just have to dig through the generic in-house labels to find them.

While there’s no official word on a Nordstrom Cyber Monday sale, our coverage over the years tells us that there most likely will be. We’ve got our ears to the ground and will be updating this story as we hear more.

#6705. Are You Ready for the ’80s Fashion Revival?

Rejoice: shoulder pads and opulence are back.

It happened suddenly: golden shades, huge shoulders, stacks of oversize jewelry. At Anthony Vaccarello’s swan song for Saint Laurent, it was all golden with big jackets, safari suits, and joyfully ruffled blouses fit for a Joan Collins-era Dynasty, but built for 2026. For spring/summer 2027, the ’80s have been a big focus. Valentino showcased jewel-toned gowns with piled-on maximalist pearls, and Giorgio Armani’s strong shoulders were straight out of a fashion history book. Mugler and Calvin Klein did strong silhouettes that alluded to the era. And even Louis Vuitton couldn’t help but look back to New York in the 1980s for its recent cruise collection, presenting models in stiff jeans and Keith Haring tops.

And why not? The ’80s were a time of experimentalism and personality, making it ripe to be mined for fashion inspiration and also less referenced than the forever hall of famer ’90s and Y2K style that fashion can’t stop loving.

The obsession has already started (or, rather, it never really ended) in the vintage world. Haile Lidow, founder of Lidow Archive, has seen a demand recently for her vintage drop waists and ruffle-skirt dresses in wild patterns. “I have so many in my collection that have gone neglected for years and are finally being noticed,” she tells ELLE. “Also, the ’80s power suits! They are back! Sometimes I update the skirt length if it feels too dated. We call it ‘minify’ but regardless, the requests for these are pouring in.”

For some, it’s about nostalgia, but for others, it’s totally new. Violet Sky, a 26-year-old Gen Z singer first became inspired to dress totally ’80s after watching the film Girls Just Want to Have Fun while she was in high school. “It was all the bright colors and just how fun everything was and the big hair,” she tells ELLE. “I just felt really drawn to it. I didn’t really have my own personal style, and so at that moment, I was like, well, why don’t I just explore this?” She started by pulling pieces from her mother and grandmother’s old wardrobe in her attic, and now exclusively wears acid-wash denim, tops bedazzled with rhinestones, and Reebok Classics every day.

“I think fashion, and interiors, and so many other aesthetic-based industries has been stuck in a really boring rut that’s been disguised as minimalism,” adds Lidow. “It started in the late ’90s as ‘chic’ and developed into an excuse for society to try less. The ’80s were the opposite: one bangle was never enough, you had to have four. Eyelids were splashed in bright colors and patterns were clashing all over the place. I think we’ve finally grown bored of the boring. We want to have fun again.”

Even fashion historians can’t help but think of the ’80s as a sort of golden age of fashion, when Vivienne Westwood and Christian Lacroix were sending highly creative pieces down the runway. Valerie Steele, director and chief curator of The Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology, even associates the era with a shoe renaissance, which we’ve also been experiencing in 2026 with the rise of It shoes. “I think what we’re seeing in part may be a hope that we can come back to a period when fashion really was fashionable, because now we’re seeing so much dissatisfaction with fashion, and with the costs of fashion, not only personally, but also to the environment, and to workers and so on,” she tells ELLE.

The familiar feeling of power dressing in the air (and on the runways) with these ’80s silhouettes is deeply tied to the female gaze. “What you see in the ’80s is that it’s coming out of a feminist movement that was growing in the ’70s, and then in the ’80s became a somewhat different feminist movement, so it was more kind of, girly, economic feminism rather than a sort of leftist, ideological feminism of the ’70s,” adds Steele. “So instead of working-class androgyny, you had suits like men had. You had powerful shoulders, you had a look of Amazonian femininity going down the runway, and that resonated with a kind of booming market, and a period when maybe, maybe feminism was becoming more commodified, or that was certainly a period when people realized that they could market specifically to women by having things that look both powerful and sexy.” Who can argue with that?

“I think that bright colors and loud fashion of the ’80s is something that’s so opposite than what’s kind of like going on today at least in everyone’s everyday life versus the runway,” adds Sky. “People are kind of intrigued about that. And they want to maybe try something different.” The ’80s revival may be nostalgic, but its appeal feels entirely of the moment: it’s instant personality in an era of sameness.

#6704. The Vogue Business Beauty Trend Tracker

The Vogue Business Beauty Tracker, produced in collaboration with Spate, tracks the top five brands, trends and ingredients that are driving the most significant positive change in year-on-year growth that have also demonstrated consistent upward growth historically. Each week, we’ll spotlight a different beauty category and the top five beauty hashtags on TikTok.

As the nights get longer, the days get colder and we move into cozy season, products and trends surrounding hydration, skin smoothing and moisturizing are growing in popularity. Moisture gloves and moisturizing socks reflect a demand for at-home moisture treatments to target the hands and feet. Brighter and more sun-kissed skin is also in demand: tinted body lotions highlight interest in moisturizers that even out skin tone with an instant or gradual tint, while turmeric body wash points to a preference for body washes that cleanse and help skin look brighter. Meanwhile, shea sugar scrub signals demand for body scrubs that combine exfoliating sugar with nourishing shea butter, with searches associated primarily with Tree Hut.

For bodycare brands, targeted solutions around the body and natural formulations are on the rise. Swarva reflects demand for body care formulated for mature and sensitive skin, with its deodorizing soap made with Japanese persimmon extract to address age-related body odor, while Anastasia Beverly Hills brings its makeup expertise to the body with its Shimmer Body Oil, a coconut-vanilla dry oil mist with a non-greasy, luminous finish. Beauty From Bees, a Canadian brand, highlights interest in small-batch, handcrafted natural products, particularly its waterless body serums made with beeswax and plant oils. Bvlgari Beauty carries the house’s signature fragrances into body care through lotions scented to match its perfumes. Finally, The Honest Company reflects interest in ingredient conscious formulations across everyday personal care essentials.

The rise in searches for #PDRNFaceMask is largely driven by Medicube bundle deals, with creators promoting discounted sets of the brand’s PDRN face masks, while #FemininePerfume shows creators reviewing and recommending fragrances positioned as feminine. #MakeupForRedHair reflects demand for makeup guidance tailored to natural and dyed redheads, with creators sharing tutorials, shade-matching advice, and product picks, while #ItchyScalpCare points to interest in routines and product recommendations for itchy scalps. Finally, #PeppermintNails highlights festive, candy cane-inspired manicures in red and white as the holiday season approaches.

It’s all about the multi-purpose fragrance this week as search data highlights growing interest in fragrances that combine practical formats, occasion-led scents, and distinctive notes. Searches for Chanel’s Coco Mademoiselle Fragrance Primer reflect demand for prep products that extend a scent’s wear, projection, and hold on the skin. Travel fragrance shows continued interest in travel-size versions of full-size scents. Meanwhile, wedding fragrance reflects demand for a dedicated signature scent for the big day, and white floral perfume highlights interest in scents built around blossoms such as jasmine, gardenia, and tuberose, while pineapple fragrance signals demand for bright, tropical fruit notes.

For fragrance brands, there is growing interest in concept-driven scents, heritage expertise, and affordable fragrance lines. Lore fragrances inspire specific memories, moods, and places, while Toskovat, an independent niche perfume house from Romania, stands out for composing each scent as a “bottled memory”, or extrait de mémoire. Shiseido reflects interest in the Japanese house’s heritage fragrances, with searches focused on Zen. Ranger Station, based in Nashville, draws on music culture and American landscapes for its unisex, artisan-style scents. Finally, Old Navy points to demand for affordable fragrance through Old Navy Beauty Co., its line of hair and body mists, lotions, and body washes, which expanded in August 2026.

It’s all about hair and nail maintenance on TikTok this week.

#KTipHairExtension reflects interest in semi-permanent extensions, with stylists showing how individual strands are bonded to natural hair using keratin tips. #CurlyHairGel and #CurlyHairVolume highlight interest in curly hair styling, from gels that keep curls defined, hydrated, and frizz-free to techniques that build lift and fullness at the root. #HolidayEyeMakeup points to interest in festive, party-ready eye looks, with tutorials circulating ahead of the winter holidays. Meanwhile, #CuticleRemover centers on at-home nail care, with videos demonstrating how to use Sally Hansen’s Instant Cuticle Remover.

At-home application and retro, graphic designs are among this month’s biggest nail trends. Searches for solid gel polish are on the rise, reflecting demand for a thicker, pot-based gel formula designed for more controlled application, while press-on sets remain popular for their reusability. White chrome powder, which creates a pearly, mirror-like finish when buffed over gel polish, is trending in time for the winter months, as well as geometric nail designs for their clean lines and shapes. Meanwhile, vintage nail polishes, including Urban Decay’s discontinued metallic foil shades, reinforce consumer interest in discontinued products that allow for a nostalgic aesthetic.

For nail brands, DIY manicure solutions, art-driven designs, and everyday nail tools are proving a success. The rise of Cyprus-based brand Doonails reflects demand for do-it-yourself manicure and pedicure products designed to deliver salon-quality results. Never Have I Ever reflects demand for reusable press-on nails featuring licensed artwork from independent artists and cultural icons, while Double Rhythm underscores interest in accessible soak-off gel polishes and nail art supplies. Heyhae offers sun-cured gel nail strips that harden naturally in sunlight without requiring a traditional UV or LED lamp, and Diamond Cosmetics signals continued interest in accessible nail products that offer variety and affordability.

Hair how-to content is ever-growing on TikTok, with creators twisting small sections of coily hair into a #coiltwist or #CurlsWithStraightener tutorials doing the rounds. Meanwhile, the rise in videos showing off #DarkBalayage points to demand for soft, dimensional color finishes on brunette and black hair, which offers a subtle look that minimizes root visibility. There’s also rising demand for lip stains that provide #AllDayLipColor, while #TestingMakeup content shows creators trying out new viral products in their full-face routines, sharing verdicts as they go.

The makeup products consumers are searching for the most are those combining precise application, long wear, and shimmering finishes. Tools such as winged eyeliner stamps take the stress and guesswork out of creating a sharp, even cat-eye look, while creamy lip liners offer buildable definition through soft, blendable formulas. Gripping primers and longwear lipsticks also reflect demand for staying power, from tacky primers that give makeup a sticky base to lip formulas designed to resist fading and transfer. Meanwhile, the rise of rose gold eyeshadow highlights interest in pink-toned metallic shades that add dimension to eye looks.

When it comes to makeup brands, lasting interest in Burberry Beauty signals the strength of luxury cosmetics from established fashion houses, especially foundations. Nude by Nature highlights demand for makeup powered by natural Australian botanicals. Beauty Creations, a Latina-founded brand, stands out for high-pigment formulas, frequent limited-edition collections, and pop culture partnerships. Sculpted by Aimee, founded by makeup artist Aimee Connolly, reflects interest in multitasking, skin-first products that simplify daily routines. Finally, KeyYou points to demand for lash extension kits and cluster lashes designed for self-application.

There’s a demand for the nostalgic on TikTok, with the #ThrowBackBeauty hashtag showing creators recreating and reviewing makeup, hair, and fashion looks from past decades. Over on #PerfumeTok, the fragrance community is reviewing, ranking, and recommending scents, while #BlackFridayBeautyDeals points to anticipation ahead of TikTok Shop’s official Black Friday campaign. Meanwhile, #FalseLashesTutorial reflects demand for step-by-step guidance on applying false lashes, and #ServerHairInspo highlights low-maintenance hairstyles built to last throughout the work shift — fueled by the viral “server hair theory” that certain styles can earn servers higher tips.

Skincare products that combine regenerative ingredients, targeted application, and everyday hydration are on the rise in search. Fresh PDRN formats — creams, face masks, and eye patches — reinforce interest in the ingredient, which is associated with cellular repair and a stronger skin barrier, as well as its use in targeted treatments like the Abib PDRN Retinal Eye Patch. Increased searches for hyaluronic acid face lotion reflects demand for deep hydration in everyday skincare, while liquid pimple patches highlight interest in subtle formulas that directly target blemishes and dry into an invisible film.

Skincare consumers are particularly intrigued in brands combining clinical-grade formulas, advanced delivery technologies, and everyday sun protection. Magic Molecule reflects continued demand for hypochlorous acid, offering a multi-purpose, FDA-cleared spray for everyday skincare. KRX Aesthetics and Meditherapy, both South Korean brands, are known for their professional skin treatments adapted for at-home use. Radical Skincare stands out for its performance-driven anti-aging formulas, powered by its proprietary Trylacel delivery technology. Finally, Invisible Zinc reflects demand for mineral-based sunscreens that use zinc oxide as the primary ingredient instead of chemical UV filters.

Over on TikTok, #DolphinSkin reflects interest in ultra-glossy, smooth, and luminous skin, specifically on the body. #GreenChromeNails and #ColorLashes highlight bold approaches to color, from mirror-like metallic manicures in shades of green to multi-colored lash looks. Content featuring #TTSKbeauty, or TikTok Shop K-beauty, shows the platform’s growing role in K-beauty product discovery. Meanwhile, the rise of #JasmineFragrance is driven by Chun Breeze Xian Jasmine, a Chinese fragrance that creators compare to the jasmine tea scent of tea house chains Molly Tea and Heytea.

In haircare, products that combine scalp support, deep nourishment, and targeted cleansing are trending in search. Peptide hair serums cater to those seeking lightweight formulas that support fuller-looking hair, with searches associated primarily with The Ordinary’s Multi-Peptide Serum for Hair Density, while hair thinning serums points to a broader focus on density and scalpcare. Rice water hair spray highlights interest in a convenient leave-in format for an ingredient valued for adding strength and shine. Cholesterol hair treatment reflects demand for rich, deep-conditioning masks that restore moisture and softness, and chlorine removal shampoo signals demand for clarifying formulas that remove chlorine build-up post-swim.

When it comes to brands, the rise of K-beauty player Lilyeve reflects demand for daily scalpcare, with searches led by its Scalp Turn Cica PDRN Brush Ampoule, a cooling leave-in treatment applied through a built-in brush head. Demand for Honeyque products highlights interest in salon-grade Japanese haircare designed to repair dry, damaged and frizzy hair, while Chāmpo stands out for blending ayurvedic principles with modern trichology, particularly through its hair serum. Bare Anatomy underscores continued demand for science-backed, dermatologically tested haircare, from anti-dandruff shampoo to a roll-on scalp serum. Finally, Brickell Men’s Products reflects interest in natural grooming formulated specifically for men.

Beyond traditional beauty content, #MakeupGame on TikTok reflects the growing overlap between beauty and gaming, with posts centered around Makeup Mania, a Roblox game where players compete through makeup and fashion looks. #HowToSilkPress and #4CWashDay highlight continued demand for textured hair education, from step-by-step silk press tutorials to wash day routines tailored to tightly coiled 4C hair. The #GlitterAcrylic hashtag points to interest in sparkling, statement acrylic nail sets, while #EczemaPatch shows the hydrocolloid format popularized by pimple patches expanding to eczema-prone skin.

In the wellness world, there’s growing interest in specialized nutrition and brands that prioritize convenience and targeted health benefits. Pure Genius Protein reflects demand for portable, high-protein formats, with ready-to-drink shots providing 23 grams of protein per serving. Sisel highlights a broad approach to wellness through dietary supplements and functional beverages, while Toplux Nutrition emphasizes science-backed supplements at affordable prices. Wip stands out for its nicotine-free caffeine pouches, offering a convenient format for an energy boost. Collectively, these brands span everyday protein intake, energy support, and targeted nutritional supplementation.

In the midst of October, #HalloweenHairClips are trending on TikTok, reflecting interest in festive, spooky hair accessories — particularly horror-themed claw clips and seasonal designs. Meanwhile, the rise of #LadybugMakeup highlights whimsical, insect-inspired makeup looks also tailored to spooky season. Across manicure content, #UglyNails are performing well, as more unconventional and unusual nail designs gain traction for allowing artistic expression, while #PinkCateyeNails reflects interest in light-reflecting cateye designs in shades of pink. The #CoilyCurly hashtag celebrates natural hair textures between curly and coily, with content focused on haircare tips and styling.

Products that combine hydration, targeted care and sensory experiences are ruling the bodycare category. Hydrating body mists meet demand for lightweight, water-like moisturizers that deliver lotion-level hydration, while anti-sweat hand creams offer targeted solutions for managing perspiration on the hands. Growing demand for hand mists suggest interest in convenient, fragrant formats that refresh and sanitize on the go, while niacinamide body wash is an example of products designed to support the skin’s moisture barrier. Finally, strawberry body scrub reflects demand for fruit-inspired bodycare that combines exfoliation with appealing scents and ingredients.

Across bodycare brands, there’s growing interest in those offering specialized and efficient approaches to personal care and grooming. Carpe reflects demand for clinical-strength sweat and odor control, while Hanni highlights simplified bodycare through “skip-step” essentials, with a particular rise in searches for its Splash Salve in-shower body balm. Proraso stands out for its Italian men’s grooming heritage. Estée Lauder has evolved its fragrance range by incorporating bodycare into its iconic scent collections, as searches for its Beautiful Perfumed Body Powder grow. Meanwhile, Prequel reflects interest in dermatologist-developed, science-backed skincare centered on skin barrier health.

This week on TikTok, the #DiscountMakeup hashtag is flooded with shoppers unexpectedly discovering Jeffree Star Cosmetics products at Dollar Tree. Meanwhile, content around #PerfumeMists is focused on reviews and recommendations of lightweight, refreshing fragrance formats. #TattooLipLiner content is also on the rise, featuring ink-like liners, peel-off stains, and semi-permanent lip treatments for long-lasting lip definition. #GlowyMakeupRoutine points to interest in luminous, radiant makeup looks and routines, while #FeatheredHair highlights interest in the ’70s voluminous, heavily layered hair look. Together, these trends highlight how beauty content is increasingly shaped by product discovery, makeup routines and nostalgic aesthetics.

There’s growing interest in fragrance trends that combine personalization, identity, and convenience. Alcohol-free fragrances, for example, reflect demand for alternative formulations to traditional perfumes, while custom perfumes point to interest in personalized scents tailored to individual preferences. The rise of masculine fragrances suggests that scent is increasingly functioning as an identity marker for male and female consumers alike, while gothic perfume reflects demand for darker and more mysterious aromatic profiles that evoke the romantic and atmospheric elements of the goth aesthetic. Finally, travel fragrances, the portable and convenient scent formats designed to make fragrance easier to pack and use on the go, are also trending.

This month, there’s particular interest in fragrance brands offering distinctive approaches to scent. Lore’s emotive, transportive fragrances translate specific moods and places into immersive scent experiences, while MCM Fragrance and Miu Miu highlight growing interest in luxury scents that extend recognizable fashion identities into fragrance, with searches for the latter mainly associated with Miutine and its youthful fragrance identity. Ranger Station stands out for its bold, high-concentration, nature-inspired scents, while Maison d’Etto offers perfumes rooted in equestrian influence, contemporary art and architecture. These brands highlight growing consumer interest in fragrance that goes beyond scent itself, offering distinctive stories, identities and sensory experiences.

As we enter October season, #SpookyNailArt is trending on TikTok, reflecting interest in Halloween-inspired nail designs based on playful motifs. Meanwhile, growing interest in the #MakeupColorTheory reinforces the rise of consumers learning about the hues that enhance their features. #ConcertHair highlights demand for hairstyles that are durable, creative and highly accessorized, specifically designed to last throughout a concert, while the #RomanticUpdo reflects interest in soft, feminine hairstyles and intentionally undone styles. #CologneHaul shows interest in discovering and showcasing fragrance purchases and collections.

When it comes to nails, there’s a growing interest in trends that combine precision, personalization, and visually distinct finishes. The Italian manicure, which creates the appearance of longer slender nails, reflects demand for more precise techniques, while nail art pens and letters on nails point to interest in customized designs and intricate details. The rise of glass nail polish highlights a preference for glossy, translucent finishes, and vibrant nails reflect demand for bold, eye-catching colors.

Among this month’s trending nail brands, there’s a clear preference for distinct approaches to at-home manicures. Reusable, press-on nail line Never Have I Ever incorporates licensed artwork from independent artists and cultural icons into nail designs, while Double Rhythm reinforces interest in accessible, soak-off gel polishes and nail art supplies for DIY and salon-style looks. IPolish stands out for its digital color-changing press-on nails, allowing users to switch between hundreds of shades using a smartphone and activation wand. Heyhae offers sun-cured gel nail strips that harden naturally in sunlight without requiring a traditional UV or LED lamp, while Sparkle & Co. specializes in DIY dip powders with unique glitters, foils, flakes, glow-in-the-dark, and color-changing effects.

TikTok is seeing an influx of content featuring #BumperBangs, reflecting interest in vintage 1940s and ’50s fringe styles consisting of a bold, rounded shape. Meanwhile, the rise of #CurlyHairBride highlights demand for bridal hair inspiration that embraces natural curls and textured styles. #WigsOnTikTok shows the growing role of TikTok in discovering, styling, and showcasing wigs. #UltaFragrance and #SephoraBeautyAdvisor highlight interest in beauty advisors sharing recommendations, product expertise and customer interactions at retailers Ulta and Sephora. Together, these hashtags highlight interest in vintage looks, occasion-specific styling, and behind-the-scenes beauty retail experiences.

There’s a growing interest in makeup products that combine ease of use, enhanced appearance, and convenient beauty benefits, according to monthly search data. Growth in creamy lip liners points to demand for smooth, easy-to-apply products that shape and define the lips, while lip volumizers help create the appearance of fuller, smoother lips without invasive treatments. Rose gold eyeshadow is also trending, driven by demand for warm, luminous shades. Gripping primer, which is a gel-based product with a tacky finish to hold your makeup in place, reflects interest in creating durable makeup looks that last throughout the day. The rise of SPF face powder reveals interest in facial sun protection beyond conventional sunscreens, with multifunctional products that both protect and control shine.

Across makeup brands, those offering distinctive products spanning various price points are performing particularly well. Hung Vanngo Beauty reflects demand for makeup artist expertise, while Burberry Beauty signals continued interest in luxury cosmetics from established fashion houses. C-beauty brand Cheeryep and Sleek Makeup highlight demand for vibrant, high-pigment makeup and innovative finishes. Maven Beauty, Fashion Nova’s makeup brand, suggests growing demand for affordable beauty options.

On TikTok, #UVHairExtensions are gaining traction, reflecting interest in innovative UV and LED hair extension techniques offering fast application, while #BrownRedHair highlights demand for rich, warm hair color combinations of brown, red, copper, and mahogany tones. Manicurist content featuring #PracticeNails shows past designs and their training progress, while #CottagecoreNails spotlights whimsical, nature-inspired manicures influenced by cottagecore aesthetics. The rise of #BridesmaidsMakeup reflects growing demand for beauty inspiration tailored to bridesmaids and wedding looks.

In skincare, monthly interest in products and treatments that combine targeted skin health benefits with gentle, barrier-supporting ingredients and advanced technologies is rising. Silicone-free sunscreen and its lightweight, ingredient-conscious sun protection is trending, while the retinol sandwich method, where retinol is layered between moisturizer to reduce the risk of irritation, is gaining traction among those looking to safely introduce retinol into their routines. There is continued demand for hyaluronic acid face lotions offering convenient, hydrating properties that support moisture retention and skin plumpness, while ceramide toners are designed to strengthen and maintain the skin barrier. Interest in high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) treatments highlights demand for advanced, non-invasive aesthetic treatments focused on skin tightening and rejuvenation.

For brands, those offering science-backed and targeted skincare solutions are trending. Elm Biosciences, which develops clinical skincare focused on healthy aging and cellular-level care, is gaining traction, while Magic Molecule offers hypochlorous acid solutions that cleanse, reduce inflammation and support skin healing. The rise of TropicSport signals demand for high-performance sun protection during active lifestyles. NewGel+ reflects interest in specialized scarcare and skin repair. The Body Shop, particularly its Drops of Youth line, highlights demand for products targeting early signs of aging while supporting skin resilience against daily environmental stressors.

On TikTok, #SheinMakeupHaul is trending, reflective of the growing interest in discovering and sharing affordable makeup products through beauty hauls. #BestHairOils shows how more consumers are comparing different hair oils and seeking product recommendations. #BakedBlush features content spotlighting new blush launches and shades comparisons through product swatches and reviews. #TinselBraids and #CakeNails highlight playful approaches to self-expression through decorative hairstyles and creative nail designs, with consumers exploring visually distinctive looks.

This month’s search data highlights growing interest in haircare products that combine targeted follicle growth with plant-based ingredients. Popular hair serums range from including specific active ingredients, with searches for redensyl and peptide serums that help reduce shedding by supporting follicle health and improving fullness, to concern-specific searches such as hair thinning serum. Rice water hairspray highlights demand for convenient, multifunctional products that can strengthen strands, add shine and reduce frizz, while plant-based shampoos reflect growing interest in products made primarily with vegan and botanical ingredients.

When it comes to haircare brands, those offering performance-driven, science-backed and premium solutions, in particular, are trending. Labo-H reflects demand for Korean scalpcare and hair loss prevention, while UltraSwim highlights interest in cleansing products designed to remove chlorine, chemical odors, and mineral buildup from hair. Bare Anatomy signals demand for science-backed haircare, addressing specific concerns such as shedding, dandruff, frizz, and damage, while Bvlgari Beauty reflects interest in luxury products combining cleansing and scalpcare with the brand’s signature scents. Meanwhile, Iso Beauty highlights growing interest in solutions that deliver salon-quality results at home.

Over on TikTok, #BabyShowerMakeup reflects interest in soft glam makeup looks tailored specifically for mothers and guests attending baby showers, while #MarchMakeup shows makeup looks based on the birthday month. #QuickCurls highlights demand for fast and easy hairstyling techniques for curly hair, while #LakeHair reflects interest in solutions to avoid or untangle the messy, textured, and sometimes dry or mineral-coated hair associated with freshwater swimming. #AntioxidantSerum shows dermatologist content discussing skincare products centered around antioxidant benefits and protection from environmental stressors.

Across wellness, monthly search data highlights growing interest in products that combine targeted benefits, convenience, and ease of use. Dopamine patches, for example, reflect demand for wearable solutions associated with mood and focus support, while acupressure wristbands reveal interest in convenient solutions for managing and preventing nausea, particularly concerning travel and motion sickness. Screenless fitness trackers demonstrate growing demand for minimalist wearable technology that passively monitors health and activity data without the distraction of a screen. Men’s fertility supplements signal interest in targeted nutritional support for male reproductive health, while liquid zinc supplements highlight demand for convenient ways to prevent or address zinc deficiency and support immune health.

For brands, there’s growing interest in those offering targeted, convenient, and science-backed wellness solutions. Pure Genius Protein reflects demand for portable, easy-to-consume protein products, while Artemis Tea highlights interest in organic herbal teas and wellness blends rooted in traditional herbalism. Nancy’s Probiotic signals demand for organic cultured foods and probiotic-focused nutrition, while EFX Sports reflects interest in performance supplements such as Kre-Alkalyn creatine, designed to support strength and recovery. The rise of Sparkle Wellness relates to continued interest in collagen supplements targeting skin, hair, nails, and overall vitality.

Over on TikTok, the growing traction for #BridalUpdoStyle reflects interest in polished, occasion-ready hairstyles for weddings and special events. #FauxBrows and #HowToSelfTan highlight different approaches to enhancing everyday beauty, from creating realistic, hair-like brow strokes to achieving an even, natural-looking tan at home. #MakeupPR reflects the influencer culture around receiving and unboxing gifted beauty products, as well as creators sharing their experiences with brands. #MakeupOver35 highlights growing interest in makeup techniques and product recommendations tailored to women over the age of 35.

In the bodycare space, current search trends highlight growing interest in products that combine targeted benefits and convenience with sensory appeal. Alpha hydroxy (AHA) body lotions and hand exfoliators reflect demand for exfoliating and smoothing products that help remove dead skin cells, dirt, and dry patches. Grape soap highlights playful, fruit-inspired formats that combine functionality with novelty and aesthetics. Epsom salt lotions reflect interest in convenient options for muscle relief and recovery, while kojic acid lotions signal demand for targeted brightening and uneven skin tone care.

As for bodycare brands, those offering targeted, skin-friendly solutions are gaining traction. QV Skincare reflects demand for sensitive skin and barrier-supportive care, while Naked Bee highlights interest in affordable, natural bodycare options incorporating ingredients such as honey, beeswax, and oatmeal. Derman points to demand for targeted antifungal treatments, and Curology reflects growing interest in dermatologist-designed solutions for body breakouts and rough texture. Meanwhile, Luna Daily highlights demand for pH-balanced, microbiome-friendly care for both the body and intimate areas. These brands reveal how the category is evolving through specialist treatments based on body area and skin concern, spanning natural-based products to dermatologist-designed solutions.

Over on TikTok, #VampNails reflect interest in bold, dramatic nail looks inspired by dark and vampy aesthetics. #RootRetouch and #GrayGrowOut highlight different approaches to managing hair color, from concealing visible roots to embracing the transition to natural gray. #HairVolumeHacks signals demand for accessible styling techniques that create fuller, more voluminous hair. #MakeupTrial reflects interest in testing and refining makeup looks ahead of weddings and special events.

This month’s search data highlights a shift toward more occasion-driven and emotionally evocative fragrance choices. The rise of wedding fragrances reflects growing interest in scents associated with meaningful celebrations and special occasions. Sport fragrances signal demand for fresh, energetic scents suited to active lifestyles and everyday wear, while sweet fragrances highlight continued preference for gourmand and indulgent scent profiles, with birthday cake perfume, for example, also offering a familiar scent evocative of childhood memories. Electric perfume, meanwhile, with searches mainly associated with the iconic Revlon fragrance from the 80s, Electric Youth, reflects the enduring appeal of discontinued scents that offer a new form of nostalgia.

When it comes to brands, DefineMe Creative Studio highlights growing interest in fragrance rooted in pop culture, with collaborations such as Barbie connecting scent with recognizable characters and cultural identities. Lore reflects demand for emotive, transportive fragrances that translate specific moods and places into scent experiences. Miu Miu and MCM Fragrance highlight growing interest in luxury scents that extend a recognizable fashion identity into the perfume space, with Miu Miu searches mainly associated with the more youthful and feminine Miutine scent. The rise of Kopari, specifically its fragrance mists, reflects demand for lighter fragrance formats suited to everyday use.

On TikTok, #CreamEyeshadowSticks are trending, as demand rises for convenient, easy-to-apply makeup formats that allow consumers to create smooth, buildable eye looks with minimal effort. #ChunkyHighlights and #NailFoils reflect growing interest in creative beauty techniques that add dimension and visual impact to hair and nails. #UltaHairSalon reflects consumers’ and salon workers’ experiences with hair services in retail stores, highlighting a convenient way to access professional salon expertise. The continued interest in #DrySkinSolutions signals demand for targeted skincare solutions focused on relieving dryness and supporting skin hydration.

There’s been a rise in search data for nail art pens, reflecting growing interest in personalized nail creativity that’s nostalgic and enables consumers to experiment with intricate and customized designs. Liquid tape reflects demand for manicure tools that simplify application while improving precision and creating cleaner, more professional-looking results. Glitter nail polish is another Y2K trend regaining momentum, with continued interest in bold, statement-making finishes that add a dose of playfulness to nail looks. The sustained demand for glass nail polish underscores the role of high-gloss translucent finishes as a more classic aesthetic. Meanwhile, celestial nails signal increasing enthusiasm for imaginative and artistic nail designs inspired by cosmic themes and metallic accents.

Nars, which phased out its nail polish line, is trending in search data, reflecting the enduring appeal of discontinued beauty products when consumers maintain connections with iconic shades and search for color dupes still available on the market. Tonic Polish and Pure Ice, meanwhile, highlight growing interest in expressive nail finishes, such as multichromes, magnetics and holographics, as well as accessible trend-driven shades, glitters and metallics that keep manicures more unique. Beyond polish, Burt’s Bees highlights growing demand for nourishing nailcare solutions, such as cuticle creams that provide hydration while supporting dry and brittle nails. Diamond Cosmetics signals continued interest in accessible nail products that offer variety and affordability.

On TikTok, #BrighteningEyeMasks reflect demand for targeted skincare solutions, with consumers using under-eye patches to depuff, hydrate, and reduce the appearance of dark circles. Content featuring #MakeupDisaster and #BadNailsCheck highlights the interest from consumers in beauty mishaps, from makeup products that fail to deliver expected results to manicure disasters and negative salon experiences. #SkincareRitual reflects interest in consistent, personalized skincare routines focused on daily maintenance. #NailTechDayInMyLife reflects interest in behind-the-scenes nail content, with consumers engaging with nail technicians’ routines, creative processes, and the realities of running a nail business. Together, these trends reflect growing consumer interest in authentic beauty experiences and personal routines.

In the makeup space, monthly data highlights growing demand for innovative, personalized, and tech-driven cosmetics. Lipstick printers, associated primarily with YSL Beauty, reflect rising interest in tech-enabled beauty personalization, allowing consumers to create customized lip shades on-demand. Aloe lipstick offers hydrating, soothing properties with pH-reactive formulas that adapt to each wearer’s lips. Soft matte lipstick reflects interest in formulas that deliver a velvety, blurred matte finish without the dryness of traditional matte lipsticks, while terracotta lipstick highlights the popularity of warm, earthy shades that offer a transeasonal beauty look. Meanwhile, ginger mascara signals growing interest in softer, natural-looking eye makeup, with this shade offering a light brown to reddish tint that subtly enhances lashes.

Prestige Cosmetics is among this month’s trending makeup brands, reflecting continued demand for accessible, high-pigment products in a broad range of colors. Hung Vanngo Beauty signals sustained interest in makeup artist-founded brands that deliver professional-quality products based on their expertise. Details by Tati signals demand for creator-led beauty brands centered on luxury makeup tools and elevated application. Black Up is a brand tailored to those looking for inclusive makeup options, offering complexion products specifically developed to enhance deeper skin tones. The enduring appeal of Burberry Beauty, meanwhile, reinforces demand for combining premium formulations with sophisticated, fashion-inspired aesthetics.

Over on TikTok, #FrizzyHairHacks and #GrayHairCare reflect growing demand for targeted hair solutions, as more consumers seek practical techniques and specialized products to manage frizz, improve smoothness, and maintain the health and vibrancy of gray and silver hair. #GoldenHourMakeup highlights demand for warm, radiant beauty looks, from golden-toned eye makeup to sun-kissed complexions with natural luminosity. The rise of the #BlondeRoots hashtag reflects continued interest in blonde hair trends that embrace visible roots, like ghost roots. #FullFaceOfDollarTreeMakeup underscores engagement in affordable beauty experimentation, with consumers creating full-face looks using accessible products.

In the skincare space, there’s growing demand for targeted, science-led solutions. Pore mousse reflects interest in innovative K-beauty cleansing formats that deeply purify and refine the appearance of pores, while silicone scar sticks demonstrate demand for convenient scar care that supports scar recovery and improves the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles. Liquid pimple patches are still rising as the next-generation blemish treatment to combine targeted ingredient delivery with an invisible, flexible finish for everyday wear. Peptide eyelash serum reflects rising interest in peptide-powered formulas that strengthen lashes and promote a fuller, healthier appearance. Meanwhile, increased searches regarding retinoid dermatitis signals the heightened awareness of managing irritation associated with active skincare ingredients.

When it comes to skincare brands, Elm Biosciences underscores growing interest in science-backed, clinically developed products, with a lab-to-patient approach focused on supporting long-term skin health and healthy aging. Caire Beauty reflects demand for hormone-aware skincare for women aged 40 to 65-plus, offering science-driven formulas designed to address the visible effects of perimenopause and menopause through advanced hydration and skin-rebuilding technologies.

Love From Yours highlights the rise of AI-powered personalized skincare, using skin analysis and lifestyle data to create customized routines tailored to individual needs. Radical Skincare represents continued interest in clinical-strength anti-aging solutions that deliver restorative results while remaining suitable for sensitive and blemish-prone skin. Scarlett Whitening, an Indonesian brand, signals growing demand for accessible, ingredient-focused skincare that combines brightening, hydrating, and acne-targeting actives.
